questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden chest pain radiating to his left arm and jaw. His electrocardiogram shows ST-segment elevation, and laboratory studies indicate elevated cardiac biomarkers. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden chest pain radiating to his left arm and jaw. His electrocardiogram shows ST-segment elevation, and laboratory studies indicate elevated cardiac biomarkers. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?

options.label: D
options.text: Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: This patient presents with acute ST-segment elevation myocardial Infarction (STEMI), which requires immediate reperfusion therapy. Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the preferred initial treatment for STEMI when performed within 90 minutes of presentation. PCI involves the insertion of a catheter into the blocked artery to open the occlusion, allowing blood flow to the heart muscle. PCI is more effective than thrombolytic therapy in improving outcomes in STEMI patients. Incorrect Options: Option A- Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery: Coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG) is an option for patients with severe and extensive coronary artery disease that cannot be treated with PCI. CABG is not the initial management for acute STEMI and is usually reserved for stable patients with chronic stable angina or unstable angina. Indications of CABG are as follows: High-grade left main stem coronary artery stenosis Significant stenosis (>70%) of the proximal left anterior descending artery, with 2-vessel or 3-vessel disease Symptomatic 2-vessel or 3-vessel disease Disabling angina despite maximal medical therapy Poor left ventricular function with myocardium that can return to function on revascularization Post Infarct angina Indications for emergency CABG Non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction with ongoing ischemia that is unresponsive to medical therapy/PCI STEMI with inadequate response to all nonsurgical therapy Significant ongoing ischemia, traumatic complications, or threatened occlusion in STEMI, after a failed PCI or previous CABG. Option C- Thrombolytic therapy: Thrombolytic therapy involves administering drugs to dissolve the clot causing coronary artery occlusion. Thrombolytic therapy is an alternative to PCI in STEMI patients who present within 12 hours of symptom onset and cannot undergo PCI within 120 minutes. However, thrombolytic therapy has a higher risk of bleeding complications than PCI and is less effective in restoring blood flow to the heart muscle. Option D- Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy: Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is a component of the initial management for STEMI patients but is not the definite treatment for acute STEMI. These medications may stabilize the patient and prevent further clot formation while awaiting PCI or thrombolytic therapy. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option B- Percutaneous Coronary Intervention:

  • This patient presents with acute ST-segment elevation myocardial Infarction (STEMI), which requires immediate reperfusion therapy. 
  • Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the preferred initial treatment for STEMI when performed within 90 minutes of presentation. 
  • PCI involves the insertion of a catheter into the blocked artery to open the occlusion, allowing blood flow to the heart muscle. 
  • PCI is more effective than thrombolytic therapy in improving outcomes in STEMI patients.

Incorrect Options: 

Option A- Coronary Artery Bypass Graft Surgery:

  • Coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG) is an option for patients with severe and extensive coronary artery disease that cannot be treated with PCI. 
  • CABG is not the initial management for acute STEMI and is usually reserved for stable patients with chronic stable angina or unstable angina.
    • Indications of CABG are as follows:
      • High-grade left main stem coronary artery stenosis
      • Significant stenosis (>70%) of the proximal left anterior descending artery, with 2-vessel or 3-vessel disease
      • Symptomatic 2-vessel or 3-vessel disease
      • Disabling angina despite maximal medical therapy
      • Poor left ventricular function with myocardium that can return to function on revascularization
      • Post Infarct angina
    • Indications for emergency CABG 
      • Non-ST segment elevation myocardial infarction with ongoing ischemia that is unresponsive to medical therapy/PCI
      • STEMI with inadequate response to all nonsurgical therapy
      • Significant ongoing ischemia, traumatic complications, or threatened occlusion in STEMI, after a failed PCI or previous CABG.

Option C- Thrombolytic therapy:

  • Thrombolytic therapy involves administering drugs to dissolve the clot causing coronary artery occlusion. 
  • Thrombolytic therapy is an alternative to PCI in STEMI patients who present within 12 hours of symptom onset and cannot undergo PCI within 120 minutes. 
  • However, thrombolytic therapy has a higher risk of bleeding complications than PCI and is less effective in restoring blood flow to the heart muscle.

Option D- Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy:

  • Medical management with antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is a component of the initial management for STEMI patients but is not the definite treatment for acute STEMI.
  • These medications may stabilize the patient and prevent further clot formation while awaiting PCI or thrombolytic therapy.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is presented because of dyspnea that occurs after exertion and he has to take rest multiple times during playing. Symptoms improve when a squatting position is assumed. A boot-like heart is seen on radiography. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy is presented because of dyspnea that occurs after exertion and he has to take rest multiple times during playing. Symptoms improve when a squatting position is assumed. A boot-like heart is seen on radiography. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Tetralogy of Fallot: Aortic and pulmonary outflows are separated by an infundibular septum and its anterior deviation during the development results in the Tetralogy of Fallot which is characterized by the following four abnormalities. Pulmonary stenosis leading to right ventricular outflow obstruction. Ventricular septal defect. Hypertrophy of the right ventricle. Ventricular septum is overridden by the aorta due to its dextroposition. The right atrium and ventricle venous return is normal but the contraction of the right ventricle shunts blood to the left ventricle through VSD due to pulmonary stenosis. Cyanosis results due to the desaturation of the blood. Symptoms like right ventricular hypertrophy and cyanosis severity depends on the degree of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Cyanosis is noted in infants with severe obstruction. In mild degrees of obstruction, infants may initially have signs of heart failure but cyanosis occurs in the first few months as the right ventricular infundibulum hypertrophies with time. Incorrect Options: Option A- Ventricular septal defect: The membranous ventricular septal defect that occurs on the anterior side of the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve in the posteroinferior position is the most common type although the defect can also occur in the muscular region of the septum. Patients with small lesions are mostly asymptomatic and at the left lower sternal border a loud harsh murmur often associated with a thrill can be heard during regular physical examination. Option C- Transposition of great vessels: It is a cyanotic cardiac abnormality in which blood normally returns to the left atrium through pulmonary veins and blood from systemic veins returns to the right atrium but the aorta arises from the right ventricle and pulmonary artery from the left ventricle. The left side of the heart receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and it is then transferred again to the lungs. The right side of the heart receives deoxygenated blood from the body and it is returned to the body through the aorta. Option D- Truncus arteriosus: In this condition, due to failure of aorticopulmonary septal development truncus arteriosus fails to divide into the aorta and pulmonary trunk, and a single arterial trunk supplies pulmonary and systemic circulations. Initial findings in the neonatal period are cyanosis and a murmur over the next few months torrential pulmonary blood flow develops, and heart failure becomes prominent. The second heart sound is single and loud. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 60-year-old female is brought to the A&E with difficulty breathing, chest pain, and hemoptysis. Her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, pulse is 120 bpm and respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute. Her oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. A pulmonary embolism is detected on CT angiography. The patient has no contraindications for thrombolysis. What is the most appropriate initial therapy for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old female is brought to the A&E with difficulty breathing, chest pain, and hemoptysis. Her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, pulse is 120 bpm and respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute. Her oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. A pulmonary embolism is detected on CT angiography. The patient has no contraindications for thrombolysis. What is the most appropriate initial therapy for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) infusion: The clinical presentation of this patient is consistent with pulmonary thromboembolism. Pulmonary thromboembolism (PTE) is a potentially life-threatening condition that occurs when a blood clot blocks one or more pulmonary arteries. The clinical presentation of PTE includes dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, tachypnea, tachycardia, and hypoxia. The patient's presentation is a medical emergency and requires prompt diagnosis and management. The most appropriate initial therapy for this patient is tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) infusion. Thrombolysis with tPA is a recommended treatment for patients with PTE who are hemodynamically unstable or have evidence of right ventricular dysfunction. The use of tPA for PTE is supported by several clinical trials that have demonstrated improved mortality and morbidity outcomes compared to anticoagulation alone. Incorrect Options: Option A- Heparin infusion: Heparin infusion is an appropriate initial therapy for patients with PTE who are hemodynamically stable. Anticoagulation with heparin is recommended as the first-line therapy for most patients with PTE, and it should be started as soon as the diagnosis is made. However, in hemodynamically unstable patients, thrombolysis with tPA is preferred over anticoagulation alone. Option C- Surgical embolectomy: Surgical embolectomy is an appropriate therapy for patients with massive PTE who are hemodynamically unstable and not responding to thrombolysis. However, surgical embolectomy is associated with a higher risk of morbidity and mortality compared to thrombolysis. It should only be considered if the patient's condition does not improve with thrombolysis. Option D- Inferior vena cava filter placement: Inferior vena cava filter placement is an appropriate therapy for patients with contraindications to anticoagulation or in whom anticoagulation has failed. It is not the most appropriate initial therapy for this patient, as she has no contraindications for thrombolysis and is hemodynamically unstable. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 79-year-old lady with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and a history of retrosternal chest tightness on exertion is evaluated using 99mTc cardiac scintigraphy. Dipyridamole is administered, and the patient experiences the same symptoms again. A second ECG reveals the leads V5 and V6 to have new ST depression and T wave inversion. Which of the following describes the indications and symptoms this patient experienced during the procedure most likely?
questions.stemHtml: A 79-year-old lady with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and a history of retrosternal chest tightness on exertion is evaluated using 99mTc cardiac scintigraphy. Dipyridamole is administered, and the patient experiences the same symptoms again. A second ECG reveals the leads V5 and V6 to have new ST depression and T wave inversion. Which of the following describes the indications and symptoms this patient experienced during the procedure most likely?

options.label: D
options.text: Ruptured atherosclerotic plaque within coronary vessels

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Dilatation of coronary vessels: Dipyridamole is a phosphodiesterase type 3 inhibitor used for treating coronary stent restenosis and intermittent vascular claudication and as an antiplatelet (anti-angina, TIA/stroke prevention) drug. Dipyridamole induces coronary vasodilation by raising adenosine levels and activating adenosine A2A receptors. Myocardial ischemia brought on by a shift of blood flow is known as coronary steal syndrome. The seriously stenotic arteries' rigidity only permits a small coronary flow reserve. Blood is therefore directed to collaterals and healthy vessels when coronary arteries widen. As a result, there is tissue ischemia distal to the coronary artery stenosis , which causes chest tightness and novel ECG abnormalities. The adenosine or dipyridamole pharmacological stress test is based on this occurrence. Incorrect Options: Option B- Increased myocardial oxygen demand: The dobutamine stress test and the cardiac exercise stress test increase myocardial oxygen demand (MVO2). Dipyridamole influences myocardial oxygenation and coronary perfusion but has minimal effects on MVO2. Option C- Vasospasm of coronary arteries: The ECG changes observed in this patient's case would be caused by the vasospasm of coronary arteries , which is the source of Prinzmetal angina. However, unlike this patient, who complained of chest tightness with exertion, Prinzmetal angina patients usually experience symptoms at rest. Dipyridamole treatment, which causes vasodilation rather than vasospasm but also causes chest pain, indicates a different reason for this patient's symptoms. Option D- Ruptured atherosclerotic plaque within coronary vessels: The mechanism that causes acute coronary syndrome (ACS), which would result in chest tightness and the ECG changes observed here, is thrombotic occlusion of a coronary vessel after the rupture of a cholesterol plaque. Every stress test carries some risk for ACS, but the risk is minimal with a dipyridamole stress test because the drug prevents platelet coagulation. A different cause probably brought on chest tightness in this patient. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency room for dizziness and palpitations for the past hour. His pulse is 185/min, and his blood pressure is 100/52 mm Hg. An ECG shows a narrow-complex, regular tachycardia without P waves. A drug activates cardiac potassium channels and causes the transient atrioventricular block. Which of the following adverse effects is most likely to occur?
questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old man presents to the emergency room for dizziness and palpitations for the past hour. His pulse is 185/min, and his blood pressure is 100/52 mm Hg. An ECG shows a narrow-complex, regular tachycardia without P waves. A drug activates cardiac potassium channels and causes the transient atrioventricular block. Which of the following adverse effects is most likely to occur?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Chest pain: The patient has been given the antiarrhythmic drug adenosine . Chest pain is a common adverse effect in patients treated with adenosine. Adenosine causes a transient atrioventricular (AV) block by increasing potassium efflux from cells, which causes hyperpolarization, decreased calcium influx, and decreased levels of intracellular cAMP. The brief AV block (usually < 15 secs) can cause chest pain and a feeling of impending doom. Other side effects of adenosine include hypotension, flushing, bronchospasm, bradycardia, and nausea. Prolonged asystole is rare but also a potential complication. Theophylline and caffeine are adenosine receptor antagonists that can inhibit the effect of adenosine. Incorrect Options: Option A- Severe headache: This statement is incorrect as severe headache is a common side effect of nitrates (e.g., nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate), which release nitric oxide in smooth muscle cells, resulting in vasodilation and increased intracranial pressure. Other side effects of nitrates include hypotension, reflex tachycardia, and syncope. Severe headaches are not a common side effect of adenosine, which this patient received. Option B- Sedation: This statement is incorrect as sedation is a known side effect of beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol, labetalol) and class IB antiarrhythmics (e.g., lidocaine, mexiletine). These lipophilic agents can penetrate the blood-brain barrier, resulting in CNS side effects. Adenosine does not cause sedation. Option D- Dry cough: This statement is incorrect as adenosine does not cause dry cough. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors can cause dry cough. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with complaints of shortness of breath and palpitations. He reports a past history of rheumatic fever during childhood. On examination, a diastolic murmur is heard at the apex, which radiates to the axilla. Echocardiography shows mitral regurgitation with prolapse of the mitral valve leaflets. Which of the following structures prevents the prolapse of the mitral valve into the left atrium?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man presents with complaints of shortness of breath and palpitations. He reports a past history of rheumatic fever during childhood. On examination, a diastolic murmur is heard at the apex, which radiates to the axilla. Echocardiography shows mitral regurgitation with prolapse of the mitral valve leaflets. Which of the following structures prevents the prolapse of the mitral valve into the left atrium?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Chordae tendineae: The chordae tendineae are cord-like tendons that attach to the papillary muscles and the edges of the mitral and tricuspid valves in the heart. They play a crucial role in preventing the prolapse of the mitral valve into the left atrium during systole. In mitral valve prolapse (MVP), the chordae tendineae may be elongated or ruptured , leading to the abnormal bulging of the mitral valve into the left atrium. This can result in mitral regurgitation, which can lead to symptoms such as shortness of breath and palpitations, as seen in this patient. Incorrect Options: Option B- Papillary muscles: The papillary muscles are small, cone-shaped muscles that are attached to the chordae tendineae and the ventricular walls. They contract during systole , pulling the chordae tendineae taut and preventing the prolapse of the mitral valve into the left atrium. However, in MVP, the papillary muscles are usually normal and the defect lies in the chordae tendineae. Option C- Tricuspid valve: The tricuspid valve is located between the right atrium and right ventricle , and is not involved in mitral valve prolapse. Option D- Aortic valve: The aortic valve is located between the left ventricle and the aorta , and is not involved in mitral valve prolapse. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D- Reentrant circuit in the right atrium: This patient with palpitations, fatigue, and an ECG showing a saw-tooth wave pattern is suggestive of Atrial flutter. Atrial flutter is an arrhythmia characterized by an ectopic re-entry circuit usually within the right atrium around the tricuspid annulus. ECG characteristics of atrial flutter include: Saw-tooth flutter waves Narrow complex tachycardia May be regular or irregular Can be associated with an AV block Management of atrial flutter is the same as atrial fibrillation: Rate control: Beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin Rhythm control: Antiarrhythmics e.g. amiodarone Anticoagulation for thromboprophylaxis Definitive treatment involves catheter ablation of the ectopic foci near the tricuspid annulus. Incorrect Options: Option A- Myocardial ischemia: Myocardial infarction presents with chest pain radiating to the left arm and neck, diaphoresis and an impending sense of doom. In MI, ECG shows ST-segment elevations rather than sawtooth waves. This relatively young patient with no risk factors is unlikely to experience a myocardial infarction. questions.stem: A 32-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency department with palpitations and shortness of breath. His heart rate is 180 beats per minute, and his ECG shows narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. He is diagnosed with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. Which of the following interventions can be used to terminate this patient’s condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency department with palpitations and shortness of breath. His heart rate is 180 beats per minute, and his ECG shows narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. He is diagnosed with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. Which of the following interventions can be used to terminate this patient’s condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Valsalva manoeuvre: Vagal manoeuvres are simple techniques used to terminate an episode of PSVT by stimulating the vagus nerve, which slows down the heart rate. These manoeuvres are safe and effective for most patients and can be performed in inpatient and outpatient settings. Some examples of vagal manoeuvres include: Valsalva manoeuvre: This involves forcefully exhaling against a closed airway ( e.g., by pinching the nose and closing the mouth) for 10-15 seconds. This increases intrathoracic pressure , stimulating the vagus nerve and slowing the heart rate. Carotid sinus massage: This involves applying gentle pressure to the carotid artery in the neck for 5-10 seconds. This can activate the baroreceptor reflex, which slows down the heart rate. Cold water immersion of the face involves splashing cold water on the face or immersing the face in cold water for a few seconds. This stimulates the trigeminal nerve, stimulating the vagus nerve and slows the heart rate. Episodes of AF are initiated by rapid bursts of ectopic beats arising from conducting tissue in the pulmonary veins or from diseased/dilated atrial tissue. Atrial fibrillation results in stasis of blood flow in the left atrium . As a result, there is an increased risk of thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage. The risk of thrombosis can be reduced by the use of anticoagulation that prevents the formation of clots that eventually lodge in the distal circulation. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Colchicine: The clinical scenario and physical findings are classical of acute pericarditis secondary to viral infection, and the drug of choice for this pregnant lady is colchicine. Acute viral or idiopathic pericarditis is a self-limiting disease of the pericardium. Non-specific and only symptomatic treatment are all that is needed for medical management of uncomplicated pericardial effusion. The first line drug in acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), i.e. aspirin or ibuprofen with or without colchicine. NSAIDs are contraindicated in pregnancy, especially in the last trimester, as is this lady, therefore the first-line treatment option for this lady is to start with colchicine. Colchicine should be continued for 3 months at a dose of 0.5mg-0.6mg orally twice daily for individuals with >70kg weight and once daily for individuals with <70kg weight. Colchicine blocks the assembly of microtubules in WBCs, thereby exerting its anti-inflammatory effects. Colchicine, especially when used with NSAIDs, is well tolerated, alleviates symptoms and decreases the incidence of recurrence. Colchicine is not approved for pyogenic and malignancy-related pericarditis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Ibuprofen: Ibuprofen is not the right agent here as it is contraindicated in pregnancy of >20 weeks. Although NSAIDs are the first-line agent for treating idiopathic and viral pericarditis but are not safe in pregnancy. These can cause oligohydramnios and patent ductus arteriosus. Option C - Prednisolone: Prednisolone is not the right option to start with in this patient. Steroids are indicated for treating recurrent pericarditis or initial-treatment failure with NSAIDs or colchicine. As this patient presents with the first episode of pericarditis with no previous treatment exposure, this is not the right drug to start. Option D - Acyclovir: Acyclovir is not the right treatment for this patient. Antiviral therapy is not recommended for treating viral pericarditis as it is a self-limiting disease. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - First diagonal branch of LAD: This patient has a high lateral ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), presenting to the emergency department in acute distress with sudden-onset chest pain during activity. Other symptoms such as diaphoresis and shortness of breath help narrow the suspicion to myocardial infarction. The ECG shows ST elevation in leads I and aVL, which are highly specific for a high lateral myocardial infarction. Reciprocal ST depression and T-wave inversion in both main inferior leads (Leads lll and aVF) are common findings due to the direction of depolarization occurring in those leads. The most common vessels occluded in a high lateral myocardial infarction are the first diagonal branch of the left anterior descending artery or, less commonly, the obtuse marginal branch of the left circumflex artery. Incorrect Options: Option A - Left coronary artery: The left coronary artery (LCA) covers a wide range of myocardial tissue. Ischemia or infarct in LCA territory would show ST-segment changes in leads l, ll, and V4-V6. Reciprocal changes may appear in aVR. These changes are not observed in this patient’s ECG. Option C - Right coronary artery: The right coronary artery (RCA) mainly supplies the SA node and the inferior aspect of the heart. It gives off the posterior descending artery in most of the population. Occlusion of the RCA would show ST-segment changes most commonly in leads ll, lll, and aVF. Option D - Posterior descending artery: The posterior descending artery (PDA) mainly supplies the AV node, posterior third of the interventricular septum, posteromedial papillary muscle, and posterior two-thirds of the ventricular wall. Findings on this ECG do not indicate a PDA occlusion, which would usually show ST-segment depression in leads V1-V4. If posterior leads were added, ST elevation would manifest in leads V7-V9. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man presented to the emergency room with complaints of palpitations and discomfort while breathing for about 30 minutes while he was sitting in his office. Past medical history is significant for occasional palpitations but less severe than this episode. He does not have any chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness. On examination, pulse is notable for irregular rhythm, with a rate of 170 beats per minute. He is vitally stable. His ECG after controlling the rate is given below. Which of the following is the most likely complication his illness can lead to?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Recurrent Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT): The most likely diagnosis in this case scenario is Wolff-Parkinson White (WPW) Syndrome The given ECG shows: A sinus rhythm A rate of 75 beats per min Short PR interval Wide QRS complexes with a slurred delta wave This is consistent with WPW Syndrome. WPW syndrome is an arrhythmia caused by an accessory electrical pathway that bypasses the AV node. The condition is usually congenital and can be associated with other cardiac defects. Symptoms : Most people with WPW syndrome are asymptomatic and are termed to have the WPW pattern on ECG. Some experience a combination of these symptoms: palpitations, tachycardia, shortness of breath, lightheadedness, or syncope and are termed to have WPW syndrome. Diagnosis : ECG : An accessory pathway allows electrical impulses to reach the ventricles more rapidly. Hence causing the characteristic: short PR interval widened QRS complexes delta waves Once the diagnosis is confirmed, other tests are performed to assess the severity of the disease and heart function. Holter monitoring Electrophysiology study Echocardiography Treatment : Medical: Orthodromic AVRT: AV nodal blocking therapy via Vagal maneuvers or drugs such as Beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, Adenosine.[1] Antidromic AVRT and Afib with preexcitation: Rhythm control with procainamide or ibutilide. Catheter ablation : A procedure in which radiofrequency waves are used to destroy the accessory pathway. Surgical : In rare cases, surgery may be required to remove the accessory pathway. Complications : The most common complication of WPW syndrome is recurrent supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). Other complications include atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, and heart failure. If left untreated, the arrhythmias from WPW syndrome can lead to hemodynamic instability, myocardial infarction and cardiac arrest . questions.stem: A 75-year-old patient is admitted to the hospital for respiratory distress and is treated for influenza. After 5 days of treatment, he continues to have a fever. On day 8, the nurse inquires about removing droplet precautions. What is the most appropriate course of action?
questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old patient is admitted to the hospital for respiratory distress and is treated for influenza. After 5 days of treatment, he continues to have a fever. On day 8, the nurse inquires about removing droplet precautions. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue droplet precautions until the fever is resolved

options.label: B
options.text: Discontinue droplet precautions since the patient finished treatment

options.label: C
options.text: Relocate the patient to a negative-pressure room

questions.answerText: Continue droplet precautions until the fever is resolved
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Continue droplet precautions until the fever is resolved Influenza is predominantly transmitted via droplets. The virus is shed from the airway and spread by coughing and sneezing. Other ways of transmission are of lesser importance. Shedding of the virus may continue despite treatment. The current recommendation indicates that droplet precautions can be dropped after 7 days from the onset of the illness or 24 hours after resolution of the symptoms (whichever is longer). In this particular example, the patient experienced a fever, so isolation precaution should be continued. Incorrect Options: Option B - Discontinue droplet precautions since the patient finished treatment: This option is incorrect because the patient still has a fever after 5 days of influenza treatment. Even though the patient completed the treatment course, the persistence of the fever suggests that the infection may not have completely resolved. Droplet precautions should be continued until the fever has resolved to prevent the potential spread of the infection to others. Option C - Relocate the patient to a negative-pressure room: This option is also incorrect. Negative-pressure rooms are typically used for patients with airborne infections, such as tuberculosis or measles, where the infectious particles can remain suspended in the air for an extended period. Influenza is primarily transmitted through respiratory droplets, not through the airborne route. Thus, relocating the patient to a negative-pressure room is not necessary in this case. Option D - Repeat treatment with Tamiflu: This option is incorrect because it assumes that the patient's fever is persisting due to an inadequate response to the initial Tamiflu treatment. However, it's important to note that some patients with influenza, especially elderly individuals or those with compromised immune systems, may experience a prolonged fever even after appropriate antiviral treatment. Repeating Tamiflu without any clinical indication may not be necessary and could lead to potential side effects without any significant benefit. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Oral valganciclovir: Antiviral treatment is indicated for infants with symptomatic congenital CMV infection (generally defined as involvement of at least one end-organ symptom). questions.stem: A 72-year-old male is admitted to the ICU for aspergillosis. Liposomal amphotericin B is ordered. Shortly after the infusion, the patient develops chills, a fever, and diffuse muscle pain. His vital signs are stable, and the infusion is continued. A day later, the patient experiences anuria. What is the most plausible reason for his anuria?
questions.stemHtml: A 72-year-old male is admitted to the ICU for aspergillosis. Liposomal amphotericin B is ordered. Shortly after the infusion, the patient develops chills, a fever, and diffuse muscle pain. His vital signs are stable, and the infusion is continued. A day later, the patient experiences anuria. What is the most plausible reason for his anuria?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Renal ischemia: Amphotericin is a highly nephrotoxic medication. The mechanism of toxicity is related to enhanced renal tubuloglomerular feedback, leading to vasoconstriction of the renal arteriole and ischemia. This causes irreversible renal ischemia and subsequent renal failure. A liposomal modification of amphotericin B has a slightly lower nephrotoxic profile than the original drug formulation. Liposomal amphotericin is also preferred to treat central nervous infections due to a slightly better penetration. Incorrect Options: Option B - Rhabdomyolysis: Rhabdomyolysis is a condition where damaged skeletal muscle tissue releases its contents, including myoglobin, into the bloodstream. Myoglobin is harmful to the kidneys and can cause acute kidney injury (AKI) when large amounts are filtered by the kidneys. While rhabdomyolysis can cause diffuse muscle pain, it is not the most plausible reason for anuria in this case. The patient's symptoms of chills, fever, and diffuse muscle pain are more likely related to the infusion of liposomal amphotericin B, which is known to cause these side effects. Option C - Dehydration: Dehydration can certainly lead to acute kidney injury (AKI), and it is important to consider fluid status in any patient with kidney dysfunction. However, in this case, the patient was just admitted, and there is no indication that he has a history of prior low fluid intake or dehydration. The most likely cause of anuria in this patient is the nephrotoxic effect of liposomal amphotericin B, leading to renal ischemia. Option D - Tubular obstruction: Tubular obstruction can occur in patients receiving certain medications, such as acyclovir, leading to acute kidney injury. However, this patient is receiving liposomal amphotericin B, not acyclovir. While amphotericin B can also cause kidney damage, it does so through renal ischemia, not tubular obstruction. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which agent is recommended for severe cases of malaria?
questions.stemHtml: Which agent is recommended for severe cases of malaria?
questions.solution: Correct Option D – Artesunate: Malaria is among the most common protozoan diseases in the world. It is an endemic disease, but in the USA, travelers can exhibit symptoms. Additionally, there are endemic areas in the USA (Florida) where malaria can be contracted due to transmission from a mosquito bite. The pharmacological approach to malaria depends on the goal of the therapy. Prophylaxis is different when treating a regular infection versus a severe infection. Treatment for malaria should not be delayed until confirmatory testing is done. Clinical suspicion is enough reason to start treatment. Pregnant women, children, and those never exposed to malaria are at particular risk. In cases of severe malaria (with multiple organ failure), artesunate is recommended. Hemolysis, prolonged QT, and mild asthma-like symptoms are the most common side effects. Incorrect Options: Option A – Quinine : It is not the first-line medication to treat malaria. Several strains of malaria are also resistant to this medication, so it is used in combination with another agent. Option B – Doxycycline : It is not the first-line medication to treat malaria. Several strains of malaria are also resistant to this medication, so it is used in combination with another agent. Option C – Ivermectin : It is used to treat river blindness, not malaria. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old female (G5 P1012) at 24 weeks of gestation presents with a productive cough, hemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, and night sweats. A chest X-ray is performed and is significant for cavitary lesions in the upper lobes of the lung bilaterally. A culture of the sputum is positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis on 3 separate occasions. Resistance testing is significant for resistance to both isoniazid and rifampin. Which of the following would be the most appropriate drug regimen for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: The patient should be put on a shortened multidrug-resistant tuberculosis regimen consisting of isoniazid (increased), ethambutol, moxifloxacin, kanamycin, prothionamide, and clofazimine.

options.label: B
options.text: The patient should be put on pyrazinamide, ethambutol, levofloxacin, amikacin, and linezolid for 6 months past consistently negative sputum samples.

options.label: C
options.text: The patient should be put on pyrazinamide, ethambutol, ofloxacin, kanamycin, and para-aminosalicylic acid for 6 months past consistently negative sputum results, followed by pyrazinamide, ethambutol, ofloxacin, and para-aminosalicylic acid for an additional 18-24 months.

options.label: D
options.text: The patient should be put on high-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, ofloxacin, kanamycin, and para-aminosalicylic acid for 6 months past consistently negative sputum results, followed by pyrazinamide, ethambutol, ofloxacin, and para-aminosalicylic acid for an additional 18-24 months.

questions.solution: Correct Option D - The patient should be put on high-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, ofloxacin, kanamycin, and para-aminosalicylic acid for 6 months past consistently negative sputum results, followed by pyrazinamide, ethambutol, ofloxacin, and para-aminosalicylic acid for an additional 18-24 months: The most appropriate regimen for a drug-resistant strain with resistance to both isoniazid and rifampin is a regimen consisting of high-dose isoniazid plus 2 drugs from the standard regimen that retain activity, plus an injectable anti-tuberculosis agent (amikacin, kanamycin), plus a fluoroquinolone (usually ofloxacin or levofloxacin), plus cycloserine, ethionamide, linezolid, or para-aminosalicylic acid for 6 months past the occurrence of consistently negative sputum cultures. This is followed by an additional 18-24 months of the prior regimen, without the injectable agent. These regimens should be administered even if the patient is pregnant. questions.solution: Correct Option D- Autonomic dysfunction and aerophobia: Rabies encephalitis is characterized by progressive central nervous system involvement. Autonomic dysfunction, including fluctuations in blood pressure and heart rate, and aerophobia (fear of air or wind) are classic features of rabies. Hydrophobia, the inability to swallow water due to painful spasms of the pharyngeal muscles, is also a hallmark symptom. Incorrect Options: Option A- Seizures and altered mental status: Seizures and altered mental status are not typical features of rabies encephalitis. Option B- Flaccid paralysis and respiratory failure: Flaccid paralysis and respiratory failure are more indicative of diseases such as botulism or certain forms of polio rather than rabies, which tends to cause hyperactivity and spasms. Option C-Hypertension and bradycardia: Hypertension and bradycardia are not characteristic of rabies. Autonomic dysregulation in rabies often leads to fluctuations in blood pressure and heart rate. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D- Granulomatosis with polyangiitis: The patient's presentation of purpura, arthralgia, weight loss, and the presence of c-ANCA is highly suggestive of Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's). This ANCA-associated small vessel vasculitis primarily affects the respiratory tract and kidneys. The classic triad includes upper and lower respiratory tract involvement, glomerulonephritis, and small vessel vasculitis. The cytoplasmic staining pattern (c-ANCA) is associated with antibodies against proteinase 3 (PR3), which is frequently positive in Wegener's. The presence of purpura and the staining pattern of ANCA are more indicative of Wegener's. Option C- Polyarteritis nodosa: Polyarteritis nodosa is a medium-sized vessel vasculitis and is not typically associated with the presence of ANCA. questions.solution: Correct Option D - In addition to blood clots, patients may present with livedo reticularis: In addition to blood clots, patients with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome may present with livedo reticularis. Livedo reticularis is a condition characterized by a mottled or net-like pattern of reddish or bluish discoloration of the skin. It is often seen in patients with antiphospholipid syndrome and can be associated with the vascular changes caused by the syndrome. Incorrect Options: Option A - Antiphospholipid syndrome only occurs concurrently with another autoimmune disorder: While antiphospholipid is seen more frequently in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) than in the general population -- and can be associated with other autoimmune diseases -- it can also occur as an isolated condition. Option B - If the diagnosis is confirmed, the patient’s immediate family members should be tested for antiphospholipid antibodies and, if positive, anticoagulated: The presence of an antiphospholipid antibody in of itself is not an indication for anticoagulation. Anticoagulation is indicated for patients with antiphospholipid antibodies who have experienced a blood clot. For such patients, lifelong anticoagulation is recommended. Given the current lack of evidence, warfarin should be used over the new generation of anticoagulants. Option C - Her obstetrician should have started anticoagulation after the patient had multiple miscarriages: In patients with obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome -- that is, women diagnosed based upon antibody titers and obstetric complications without a prior blood clot -- there is inadequate data to recommend anticoagulation to prevent the occurrence of the first thrombosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following does not correspond to brainstem death?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following does not correspond to brainstem death?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Absence of toe jerk: Brain death is when functional brainstem death occurs permanently such that consciousness and spontaneous respiration are impossible . Certain preconditions have to be met for the diagnosis of brain death: The patient must have undergone severe brain damage of known cause Is highly unconscious and unresponsive Requires ventilation No known CNS depressants and muscle relaxants are causing the clinical presentation. Absence of low body temperature, severe hypotension and metabolic or hormonal pathologies With the satisfaction of preconditions, a formal assessment of the brainstem reflexes can be performed. These are to be performed by two clinicians not associated with the transplant team on two separate occasions. The absence of cranial reflexes, motor responses, and spontaneous respiration characterises brain death. An absence of a motor response to painful stimuli to the head/face or within the cranial nerve distribution to adequate stimulation of any somatic area indicates brainstem death. Spinal reflexes such as toe or finger movements do not indicate brainstem death. Incorrect Options: Option A - Absence of pupillary reflex: The absence of cranial nerve reflexes characterises brainstem death. These reflexes are: Pupillary Corneal Gag (pharyngeal) Tracheal (cough) Oculovestibular (caloric) Option B - Absence of spontaneous respiration: The absence of spontaneous respiration characterises brainstem death which is checked in the following manner: Pre Ventilation with 100% oxygen is given for a minimum of 5 minutes. Then, the patient is detached from the ventilator for 10 minutes to confirm the absence of respiration. During this time, the arterial PO 2 must be >8kPa (60 mmHg ) to ensure adequate respiratory stimulation. 6L/min oxygen is delivered through the endotracheal catheter to prevent hypoxia during the apnoea. Option D - Absence of cough: A cough or tracheal reflex is a cranial reflex which characterises brainstem death. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option C - Absence of toe jerk:

  • Brain death is when functional brainstem death occurs permanently such that consciousness and spontaneous respiration are impossible.
  • Certain preconditions have to be met for the diagnosis of brain death:
    • The patient must have undergone severe brain damage of known cause
    • Is highly unconscious and unresponsive
    • Requires ventilation
    • No known CNS depressants and muscle relaxants are causing the clinical presentation.
    • Absence of low body temperature, severe hypotension and metabolic or hormonal pathologies
  • With the satisfaction of preconditions, a formal assessment of the brainstem reflexes can be performed.
  • These are to be performed by two clinicians not associated with the transplant team on two separate occasions.
  • The absence of cranial reflexes, motor responses, and spontaneous respiration characterises brain death.
  • An absence of a motor response to painful stimuli to the head/face or within the cranial nerve distribution to adequate stimulation of any somatic area indicates brainstem death.
  • Spinal reflexes such as toe or finger movements do not indicate brainstem death.

 

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Absence of pupillary reflex:

  • The absence of cranial nerve reflexes characterises brainstem death.
  • These reflexes are:
    • Pupillary
    • Corneal
    • Gag (pharyngeal)
    • Tracheal (cough)
    • Oculovestibular (caloric)

Option B - Absence of spontaneous respiration:

  • The absence of spontaneous respiration characterises brainstem death which is checked in the following manner:

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Fusobacterium nucleatum: The most common anaerobic species in pulmonary empyemas was found to be Fusobacterium nucleatum, which are small spindle shaped organisms frequently present in gum disease and contributes to dental plaque formation. The organism is known for its characteristic to adhere to both type IV collagen and other microorganisms, and is the most likely oral bacterium to be involved in infections in distant sites of the body. Incorrect Options: Option A - Microaerophilic streptococci: Though slightly less common than fusobacterium, is a frequent pathogen involved in parapneumonic effusions and empyemas and more often than not is a component of a polymicrobial infection with anaerobes and aerobes. Option C - Prevotella: Is a non-motile, anaerobic, gram negative rod which is part of the normal flora of the mouth and is involved in gingival disease. The species has the propensity to cause infections at distant sites of the body, especially the lungs through aspiration. Option D - Bacteroides species: Are anaerobic gram negative rods, and are a component of the normal flora of the gut. They have the potential to cause abscesses throughout the body. The most common species encountered in the laboratory is B. fragilis, which are susceptible to carbapenems and metronidazole yet have a high rate of resistance to penicillin, cefoxitin, clindamycin, and fluoroquinolones. @Neet_pg_bot

The patient has a recent history of a family member who had contracted tuberculosis. Which of the following characteristics of the pleural fluid would be characteristic of infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male presents with a right sided hydrothorax. The pleural fluid is drained and sent for pathological analysis. The patient has a recent history of a family member who had contracted tuberculosis. Which of the following characteristics of the pleural fluid would be characteristic of infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
questions.solution: Correct Options A - Adenosine deaminase (ADA) > 40 U/L: Tuberculosis may present with pleural effusions, which characteristically are composed of a majority of lymphocytes. ADA positivity > 40 U/L makes the infection with tuberculosis more likely, though the finding may be found in malignancies and chronic inflammation. Incorrect Options: Option B - pH < 7.2, lactate dehydrogenase (LD) > 700, and glucose <30: These findings are characteristic of a pleural effusion due to rheumatoid arthritis. These parameters indicate a severe systemic inflammatory response which is not typically associated with tuberculosis. Option C - pH < 6.0: This is an unusually low pH for any type of pleural effusion and is more typically associated with an esophageal perforation leading to the leakage of gastric contents into the pleural space. This is not a typical finding in tuberculosis. Option D - pH < 7.2 with >100,000 neutrophils/mL: This is indicative of a purulent infection, or empyema, in the pleural space. While tuberculosis is an infection, it typically does not cause a purulent effusion and instead leads to a lymphocytic exudative effusion. Therefore, a high neutrophil count is not typically associated with tuberculosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Disconnect ventilator: Asthmatic patients can be difficult to manage on the ventilator. They are prone to air-trapping and auto-PEEP, which can lead to hemodynamic collapse. Smaller tidal volumes, lower respiratory rates, and decreased inspiratory:expiratory ratios can minimize this risk. The first step in a decompensating asthmatic patient on the ventilator is to de-connect from the vent and allow any air trapped in the lungs to escape. Often, there is an audible exhalation from the ET tube, and the patient’s hemodynamics will improve. Chest examination reveals hyperinflation, wheezing, and prolonged expiration. What is the most likely complication of asthma in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Acute exacerbation: Acute exacerbation of asthma is a sudden and severe worsening of asthma symptoms, which can be life-threatening. It can be triggered by various factors such as exposure to allergens, infections, exercise, emotional stress, and medication non-adherence. The symptoms of acute exacerbation of asthma may include wheezing, shortness of breath, coughing, chest tightness, and difficulty in breathing. During an acute exacerbation, the airways become inflamed, swollen, and narrowed, making it difficult for air to move in and out of the lungs. This can result in a decrease in oxygen saturation and a rise in carbon dioxide levels in the blood, leading to respiratory failure in severe cases. Incorrect Options: Option A - Pneumonia: While patients with asthma may be at increased risk for developing pneumonia, the scenario does not provide any indication that the patient has an infection or signs of pneumonia on examination. Option B - Pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary embolism is a life-threatening condition that can cause shortness of breath, chest pain, and cough, but it is not a common complication of asthma and is unlikely to be the cause of the patient's symptoms based on the scenario. Option D - Bronchitis: Bronchitis is a respiratory condition that is characterized by inflammation of the bronchial tubes and can cause cough, chest discomfort, and shortness of breath. However, it is not the most likely complication of asthma in this scenario, as the patient's symptoms and signs are more consistent with an acute exacerbation of asthma. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 36-year-old male presents to the clinic with a complaint of severe shortness of breath. The patient never smoked and is also seeking treatment with a hepatologist for liver issues. On examination, a prolonged wheeze is appreciated. Spirometry is performed and forced expiratory volume in the first second after the bronchodilator is 65% of the predictive value. A clinical diagnosis of emphysema is made. The patient inquires about the cause of the disease at this young age. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.stemHtml: A 36-year-old male presents to the clinic with a complaint of severe shortness of breath. The patient never smoked and is also seeking treatment with a hepatologist for liver issues. On examination, a prolonged wheeze is appreciated. Spirometry is performed and forced expiratory volume in the first second after the bronchodilator is 65% of the predictive value. A clinical diagnosis of emphysema is made. The patient inquires about the cause of the disease at this young age. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a protease inhibitor which is synthesised by the liver. It inactivates the neutrophil elastase and protects the lung tissue. It is caused by a genetic mutation which causes a conformational change in the structure of alpha-1 antitrypsin. The dysfunctional protein affects the liver by accumulating in the hepatocytes' endoplasmic reticulum resulting in hepatitis and liver cirrhosis. In the lungs, its deficiency results in an uninhibited activity of neutrophil elastase, which causes pulmonary parenchyma destruction and results in pan acinar emphysema. Patients are < 60 years of age. Incorrect Options: Option B - Smoking Nicotine and smoking cause the inactivation of protease inhibitors and form reactive oxygen species. Smoking results in the destruction of respiratory bronchioles, resulting in centrilobular emphysema. Option C - Bullae formation In giant bullous emphysema, large bullae are formed, which cause the destruction of surrounding pulmonary tissue. Option D - Scar formation The chronic inflammation results in scar formation due to quartz exposure which results in cicatricial emphysema. @Neet_pg_bot

  • In the lungs, its deficiency results in an uninhibited activity of neutrophil elastase, which causes pulmonary parenchyma destruction and results in pan acinar emphysema. 
  • Patients are < 60 years of age. 

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Smoking 

  • Nicotine and smoking cause the inactivation of protease inhibitors and form reactive oxygen species.  
  • Smoking results in the destruction of respiratory bronchioles, resulting in centrilobular emphysema. 

Option C - Bullae formation 

  • In giant bullous emphysema, large bullae are formed, which cause the destruction of surrounding pulmonary tissue. 

Option D - Scar formation 

  • The chronic inflammation results in scar formation due to quartz exposure which results in cicatricial emphysema.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a systemic side effect after prolonged use of ipratropium?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a systemic side effect after prolonged use of ipratropium?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Urinary retention Up to 20% of ipratropium can be absorbed given as MDI can be absorbed via mucosal membranes of the mouth or systemic absorption through the pulmonary circulation. Consequently, some systemic side effect can be possible. Anticholinergic agents are known to cause urinary retention. In pooled analyzed of 19 randomized trial symptoms of urinary retention was more frequently present in a patient taking inhaled anticholinergic that control group. On the other hand UPLIFT trial showed no-statistically significant increase in the rate of urinary retention. Finally, in small trial 25 patient with BPH, no exacerbation of symptoms was noted. Consequently, the patient should be counseled that urinary retention might occur, but it is not universal complication. Incorrect Options: Options B - Immunosuppression: This is not a typical side effect of anticholinergic medications such as ipratropium. Immunosuppression is more commonly seen with long-term use of corticosteroids, which can suppress the body's immune response. Options C - Dry mouth: While it is true that anticholinergic medications can cause dry mouth, this is typically a local side effect due to the medication acting on the muscarinic receptors in the salivary glands to reduce saliva production. However, in the case of inhaled ipratropium, the medication is mainly acting on the receptors in the lungs and not the salivary glands. Therefore, while dry mouth can occur, it is less common and generally not considered a systemic side effect. Option D - Hair loss: Hair loss is not a known side effect of anticholinergic medications like ipratropium. Hair loss can occur due to various reasons, including genetics, certain diseases, stress, and the use of certain medications, but ipratropium is not known to cause this. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man is evaluated for increasing shortness of breath. He can no longer walk up a flight of stairs without stopping. He denies fevers, coughing, chest pain or pressure, palpitations, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Cardiovascular examination is unremarkable. There is no jugular venous distention or lower extremity edema. Pulmonary examination is unremarkable. He is a nonsmoker and a retired roofer. Which of the following statements concerning asbestos-induced lung disease is accurate?

There is no jugular venous distention or lower extremity edema. Pulmonary examination is unremarkable. He is a nonsmoker and a retired roofer. Which of the following statements concerning asbestos-induced lung disease is accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Asbestos exposure increases the risk of lung cancer associated with cigarette smoke exposure

options.label: B
options.text: Coughing, sputum production, and wheezing are the most common presenting symptoms

options.label: C
options.text: Antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate have prognostic implications

options.label: D
options.text: Cigarette exposure does not increase the risk of lung cancer associated with asbestos exposure

questions.answerText: Asbestos exposure increases the risk of lung cancer associated with cigarette smoke exposure
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Asbestos exposure increases the risk of lung cancer associated with cigarette smoke exposure: The risk of lung cancer associated with exposure to both asbestos and cigarette smoke appears to be multiplicative. A 1979 report in the Annals of the New York Academy of Science showed that asbestos is associated with a 6-fold increase, cigarette smoking with an 11-fold increase, and both cigarette smoke and asbestos exposure with a 59-fold increase in the risk of lung cancer. Incorrect Options: Option B - Coughing, sputum production, and wheezing are the most common presenting symptoms: Coughing, sputum production, and wheezing are not the most common presenting symptoms of asbestos-induced lung disease. The most common presenting symptom of asbestos-induced lung disease is dyspnea, which can be a result of interstitial lung disease (asbestosis) or lung cancer. Asbestos exposure primarily affects the lungs' interstitium, leading to fibrosis and scarring, which can cause progressive dyspnea. Option C - Antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate have prognostic implications : Antinuclear antibody (ANA), rheumatoid factor (RF), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) are not specific markers for asbestos-induced lung disease. These are nonspecific laboratory tests and are not used for diagnosing or prognosticating asbestos-related lung conditions. Asbestosis and asbestos-related lung diseases are diagnosed based on clinical history, occupational exposure, radiographic findings, and pulmonary function tests. Option D - Cigarette exposure does not increase the risk of lung cancer associated with asbestos exposure : Cigarette exposure does increase the risk of lung cancer associated with asbestos exposure. Both asbestos exposure and cigarette smoking are independent risk factors for the development of lung cancer. When a person is exposed to both asbestos and cigarette smoke, the risk of lung cancer is synergistically increased. As mentioned in the correct answer, the risk of lung cancer associated with exposure to both asbestos and cigarette smoke appears to be multiplicative. @Neet_pg_bot

On physical examination, there are decreased breath sounds on the left side. A chest X-ray shows a collapsed left lung. Which one of the following would be the ideal first-line treatment for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 24 years old man with sudden onset left-sided chest discomfort and breathing difficulties arrives at the emergency department. He is a smoker and has an asthmatic. On physical examination, there are decreased breath sounds on the left side. A chest X-ray shows a collapsed left lung. Which one of the following would be the ideal first-line treatment for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Chest tube placement: The clinical situation fits the description of a pneumothorax, a condition marked by the air in the pleural cavity. A pneumothorax can be either spontaneous or traumatic, and the severity can range from mild to life-threatening. The initial treatment for a pneumothorax is determined on its size and severity. A moderate to large pneumothorax is likely the cause of the patient's rapid onset chest discomfort and shortness of breath in this case. This diagnosis is also supported by the physical examination finding of diminished breath sounds on the left side. The appearance of a collapsed left lung on a chest X-ray confirms the diagnosis of a pneumothorax. The initial course of action is to insert a chest tube. In order to allow for the drainage of air and re-expansion of the lung, a tube is inserted into the pleural space in this procedure. Chest tube placement is the most effective and definitive treatment for a moderate to large pneumothorax. Incorrect Options: Option A - Needle Aspiration: Needle aspiration is a less invasive procedure than chest tube placement and can be used to treat a small pneumothorax. However, it is not appropriate for a moderate to large pneumothorax. Option C - Observation with supplemental oxygen: Observation with supplemental oxygen may be appropriate for a small pneumothorax that is not causing significant respiratory distress. However, in this case, the patient is experiencing significant symptoms and has a collapsed lung, which indicates the need for more aggressive management. Option D - Administration of bronchodilators: Bronchodilators are not recommended for the treatment of a pneumothorax. Despite the patient's asthma history, the findings of the physical exam and the chest X-ray indicate a pneumothorax as the cause of his symptoms. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Start the patient on 4 drug intensive phase treatment
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Start the patient on 4 drug intensive phase therapy: This patient has clinical features consistent with Active pulmonary tuberculosis, including a persistent cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, a left upper lobe infiltrate on chest x-ray, and AFB seen on sputum microscopy. A positive Mantoux tuberculin skin test further supports the diagnosis. The most appropriate next step in management is to start the patient on 4 drug therapy for 2 months (intensive phase). Recommended first line treatment includes isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. This is followed by continuation phase treatment with isoniazid and rifampin for 4-6 months. Incorrect Options: Option A - Start the patient on isoniazid therapy alone: Isoniazid monotherapy is not recommended due to the risk of developing resistant strains of mycobacterium tuberculosis. Option C - Refer the patient to a specialist for further evaluation: It may be appropriate in certain cases, especially in complicated cases, but in this case, the patient can be managed by a primary care provider. Option D - Start the patient on pyrazinamide and ethambutol therapy: Pyrazinamide and ethambutol are typically used in combination with isoniazid and rifampin during intensive phase therapy but not in isolation. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: C

questions.answerText: Dilation of bronchi with thickened walls
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Dilation of bronchi with thickened walls: The defining morphological characteristic of Bronchiectasis is the dilation of bronchi with thickened walls. Bronchiectasis is a chronic respiratory disease characterized by the irreversible dilation and thickening of the bronchial walls due to recurrent infections, inflammation, or obstruction. This leads to the accumulation of mucus and impaired clearance, leading to recurrent lung infections and chronic cough. The dilation of bronchi can be seen in imaging studies like chest X-rays, CT scans, or bronchograms Incorrect Options: Option B - Increased numbers of alveoli in the lungs: Increased numbers of alveoli in the lungs is not a morphological characteristic of Bronchiectasis because Bronchiectasis is a condition that primarily affects the bronchi, which are the large airways that lead from the trachea to the lungs Alveoli are small air sacs within the lungs where gas exchange occurs. They are not directly affected by Bronchiectasis, although if the condition is severe and chronic, it can eventually damage the alveoli and other lung structures. The primary morphological characteristics of Bronchiectasis are related to the bronchial walls, including dilation, thickening, and scarring. Option C - Presence of fluid-filled cavities in the lungs: Presence of fluid-filled cavities in the lungs is not a defining morphological characteristic of Bronchiectasis. Cysts or cavities are sometimes observed in patients with Bronchiectasis, but this is not always true. Option D - Presence of nodules in the lungs: Presence of nodules in the lungs is not a defining morphological characteristic of Bronchiectasis. Nodules may be seen in patients with other lung conditions, such as tuberculosis or lung cancer. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Length-time bias: Length-time bias is an error which occurs due to measuring a time interval which is to short, possible over-representing longer disease processes. This error is especially applicable to lung cancers, which have a wide variability of growth rates. Incorrect Options: Option A - Centripetal bias: Centripetal bias occurs when a study cohort is analyzed through a specific institution or center that may not be representative of the broader population. This can lead to biased results that may not be applicable to the general population. Option B - Lead-time bias: Lead-time bias occurs when a disease is detected earlier through screening or diagnostic tests, but this early detection does not necessarily lead to improved outcomes. This bias can make it appear that a screening test is effective in prolonging survival, when in fact, it may only be detecting the disease earlier without providing any actual benefit in terms of survival. Option D - Reporting bias: Reporting bias refers to the selective inclusion or exclusion of results in a study, which can lead to a distortion of the true relationship between variables. This bias can arise if researchers or journals choose to publish only positive or significant results, while neglecting to publish negative or non-significant findings. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best reflects our current understanding of the physiology of the pleural space?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements best reflects our current understanding of the physiology of the pleural space?

options.label: A
options.text: Absorption of pleural fluid is effectuated by uptake by capillaries

options.label: B
options.text: Liquid, proteins, and other molecules are actively transported through mesothelial cells into the pleural space

options.label: C
options.text: Pressure gradient between the pleural space and interstitial space in which the intrapleural pressure > interstitial pressure

options.label: D
options.text: Molecules, proteins, and liquid move passively

questions.answerText: Molecules, proteins, and liquid move passively
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Molecules, proteins, and liquid move passively: The pleural space consists of two cellular layers, a superficially located mesothelial layer and an underlying connective tissue layer. These membrane have been shown to be leaky, enabling the occurrence of passive movement of molecules, proteins, and liquid. Incorrect Options: Option A - Absorption of pleural fluid by capillary uptake: Pleural fluid absorption is mainly carried out through lymphatic vessels in the parietal pleura, not capillaries. The movement of fluid into the capillaries is driven by oncotic pressure rather than by an active process. Option B - Active transport of liquid, proteins, and other molecules through mesothelial cells: The mesothelial cells in the pleura do not actively transport liquid, proteins, and other molecules into the pleural space. Fluid accumulation in the pleural space is primarily due to alterations in hydrostatic and oncotic pressures, and the permeability of the pleura, allowing for passive flow. Option C - Pressure gradient between the pleural space and interstitial space where the intrapleural pressure is greater than the interstitial pressure: This is not accurate. The pressure within the pleural space (intrapleural pressure) is generally negative (or less than atmospheric pressure) to maintain lung expansion. It's not greater than the interstitial pressure. The negative pressure facilitates the passive flow of fluid from the interstitial space into the pleural space. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 30-year-old male presents to the clinic with complaints of fatigue, weakness, and a feeling of fullness in the left upper quadrant of his abdomen. On physical examination, the spleen is palpable well below the left costal margin. Laboratory tests reveal normocytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. The patient denies any recent infections or travel history. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for the patient's symptoms and findings?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old male presents to the clinic with complaints of fatigue, weakness, and a feeling of fullness in the left upper quadrant of his abdomen. On physical examination, the spleen is palpable well below the left costal margin. Laboratory tests reveal normocytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. The patient denies any recent infections or travel history. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for the patient's symptoms and findings?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Gaucher disease: Gaucher disease is a rare genetic disorder caused by the deficiency of an enzyme called glucocerebrosidase, leading to the accumulation of a substance called glucocerebroside in cells, particularly macrophages. This buildup can cause enlargement of the spleen (splenomegaly) and may result in symptoms like fatigue, weakness, and a feeling of fullness in the abdomen due to the enlarged spleen. Laboratory findings can include anemia and thrombocytopenia due to the sequestration of blood cells in the spleen. Incorrect Options: Option A - Rheumatoid arthritis: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disorder primarily affecting the joints. It typically does not cause symptoms like fatigue, weakness, or splenomegaly (enlarged spleen). Laboratory findings in rheumatoid arthritis are more focused on autoimmune markers and inflammatory markers rather than anemia and thrombocytopenia. Option B - Infectious mononucleosis (EBV): Infectious mononucleosis, caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), can lead to symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, and splenomegaly. However, the key differentiating feature in this case is the presence of normocytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. These findings are not characteristic of EBV infection. Option C - Thalassemia major: Thalassemia major is a genetic disorder characterized by abnormal hemoglobin production, leading to chronic anemia. While it can cause fatigue and weakness due to the anemia, it typically does not result in a palpable spleen well below the left costal margin. Thalassemia major is not associated with thrombocytopenia or a feeling of fullness in the abdomen. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatrician with complaints of severe eczema, recurrent pyogenic infections, and bleeding episodes. Physical examination reveals eczematous skin lesions, petechiae, and small platelets on peripheral smear. Laboratory tests show low IgG and IgM levels, along with increased IgE and IgA. Which of the following immunodeficiency syndromes is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatrician with complaints of severe eczema, recurrent pyogenic infections, and bleeding episodes. Physical examination reveals eczematous skin lesions, petechiae, and small platelets on peripheral smear. Laboratory tests show low IgG and IgM levels, along with increased IgE and IgA. Which of the following immunodeficiency syndromes is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome is an X-linked immunodeficiency disorder characterized by the triad of eczema, recurrent infections, and thrombocytopenia (low platelet count). Patients with Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome often have bleeding episodes due to the combination of low platelet counts and platelet dysfunction. They also have increased IgE levels, which can contribute to the development of eczema. The syndrome is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome protein (WASP), which plays a crucial role in cytoskeletal organization and immune cell function. Incorrect Options: Option A - X-Linked Bruton's Disease (X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia): X-Linked Bruton’s Disease, also known as X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA), is characterized by a deficiency in B cells and a lack of antibodies (IgG, IgA, and IgM). However, the presentation described in the question includes increased levels of IgE and IgA, which is not consistent with XLA. In XLA, patients would be prone to recurrent bacterial infections but would not have bleeding episodes or increased IgE levels. Option B - X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA): This is not the correct answer for the reasons mentioned above. XLA is characterized by low levels of all immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, and IgM) due to a lack of mature B cells. Option C - Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID): SCID is characterized by severe defects in both T and B cell function, resulting in a profound immunodeficiency. Patients with SCID typically present with severe and recurrent infections from a very young age. The presentation described in the question includes eczema, bleeding episodes, and increased IgE levels, which are not typical of SCID. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 44-year-old female with suspected myasthenia gravis is planned for robotic thymectomy under general anesthesia. During the preoperative anesthesia evaluation, he related a history of recurrent pulmonary aspiration and significant ocular weakness. Which of the following antibodies are likely to be present in the plasma and can be used for preoperative screening of myasthenia gravis?
questions.stemHtml: A 44-year-old female with suspected myasthenia gravis is planned for robotic thymectomy under general anesthesia. During the preoperative anesthesia evaluation, he related a history of recurrent pulmonary aspiration and significant ocular weakness. Which of the following antibodies are likely to be present in the plasma and can be used for preoperative screening of myasthenia gravis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Anti-muscle-specific kinase antibodies: Postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor antibodies are the most common antibodies found in patients with myasthenia gravis. These antibodies are present in nearly 95% of patients diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. Other groups of patients with significantly higher involvement of bulbar muscles have muscle-specific kinase antibodies. These antibodies occur in nearly 50% of patients with myasthenia gravis. They are produced against the phosphorylating enzyme in the skeletal muscles. Their role is defined in patients with bulbar involvement or in patients seronegative for anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. The sensitivity is in the following order: acetylcholine receptor (postsynaptic) > muscle-specific kinase antibodies. Incorrect Options: Option A - Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies (pre-synaptic): Unlike Lambert-Eaton syndrome where the antibodies are against presynaptic calcium channels, myasthenia is primarily a postsynaptic disorder. Antibodies are produced against postsynaptic receptors or muscle-specific kinase. This describes the presynaptic antibody, which is not related to myasthenia. Option B - Anti-acetylcholinesterase antibodies: Acetylcholinesterase is an enzyme that metabolizes the acetylcholine released in the synaptic cleft. Destruction of this enzyme would produce symptoms similar to organophosphate poisoning. This would lead to increased activity of both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. Myasthenia is primarily a disease of nicotinic receptors, and these antibodies have no relation to myasthenia gravis. Option D - Anti-thymocyte globulin antibodies: Patients with thymoma have a high incidence of myasthenia gravis. This has been attributed to a T-cell-mediated autoimmune response observed in patients with hyperactive thymus. This, however, is not related to anti-thymocyte globulin antibodies. These antibodies are therapeutically used in patients who receive transplanted organs and are used for immunosuppression. @Neet_pg_bot
