questions.stem: A first-time mother presents with her 9-day-old infant who has experienced seizures. The infant had an uncomplicated term delivery and has been otherwise well. The infant has been and remains afebrile. The mother reports diluting the baby's formula. What is the most likely cause of this infant's seizures?
questions.stemHtml: A first-time mother presents with her 9-day-old infant who has experienced seizures. The infant had an uncomplicated term delivery and has been otherwise well. The infant has been and remains afebrile. The mother reports diluting the baby's formula. What is the most likely cause of this infant's seizures?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Hyponatremia: In a well newborn without a fever, hyponatremia is the most common cause of seizures. Water intoxication is the most common cause of hyponatremia during infancy. Infants are unable to concentrate urine adequately, so parents who dilute formula or give their infants tap water put their infants at risk. Other causes of neonatal seizures also include neonatal encephalopathy and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, structural brain injuries, including ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke; glucose or other electrolyte abnormalities; and systemic or CNS infections. In a well-baby, a genetic epilepsy syndrome such as benign familial neonatal epilepsy may be the cause. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hypokalemia: Hypokalemia is uncommon in infancy and does not typically cause seizures. Option C - Hypocalcemia: Hypocalcemia is also a common cause of seizures in neonates, so serum calcium levels should be checked. In fact, all infants have a slight decline in serum calcium levels with a nadir at 24 to 48 hours. Symptomatic hypocalcemia is more common in infants of diabetic mothers, preterm infants, or infants with a history of anoxic encephalopathy. Option D - Hypomagnesemia: Hypomagnesemia is not as common as hypocalcemia, but symptoms of hypomagnesemia mimic those of hypocalcemia. It is difficult to correct hypocalcemia if the serum magnesium is also low. Therefore, infants with seizures should have a comprehensive evaluation of their electrolytes. @Neet_pg_bot

He undergoes successful coiling of the aneurysm. On hospital day 10 he suddenly developed right gaze preference, left face and arm weakness, and left hemineglect. If the right middle cerebral artery were insonated by Transcranial Doppler what values would you expect?

If the right middle cerebral artery were insonated by Transcranial Doppler what values would you expect?

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.answerText: Elevated flow velocity and elevated Lindegaard ratio
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Elevated flow velocity and elevated Lindegaard ratio: Transcranial Doppler can be used to screen for subarachnoid hemorrhage-related cerebral vasospasm. In general, cerebral vasospasm results in an increase in flow velocities. Sensitivity and specificity vary depending on the thresholds used. Flow velocity >120 cm/sec in the middle cerebral arteries is commonly considered abnormal. Flow velocity >200 cm/sec in the middle cerebral artery often suggests severe vasospasm. The Lindegaard ratio (middle cerebral artery velocity/internal carotid artery velocity) can also be used to assess for cerebral vasospasm. A Lindegaard ratio of <3 is usually considered normal. A Lindegaard ratio > 6 suggests severe vasospasm. Incorrect Options: Option A - Elevated flow velocity and reduced Lindegaard ratio: This option suggests that in the context of the patient's presentation with neurological deficits after coiling of a ruptured anterior communicating artery (ACoA) aneurysm if the right middle cerebral artery (MCA) were insonated by Transcranial Doppler (TCD), the flow velocity in the MCA would be elevated. This elevation in flow velocity could be due to the presence of high-velocity turbulent blood flow caused by vasospasm, which is a common complication following subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) and aneurysm rupture. Option B - Reduced Flow Velocity and Reduced Lindegaard Ratio: In the context of a ruptured anterior communicating artery (ACoA) aneurysm, the sudden development of right gaze preference, left face and arm weakness and left hemineglect on hospital day 10 would be suggestive of a new-onset ischemic stroke. In this case, if the right middle cerebral artery (MCA) were insonated by Transcranial Doppler (TCD), the flow velocity in the MCA would likely be reduced due to the occlusion or significant stenosis of the artery supplying blood to that territory. The Lindegaard ratio (MCA velocity/internal carotid artery velocity) could also be reduced, indicating reduced flow in the MCA. Option C - Reduced Flow Velocity and Elevated Lindegaard Ratio: This combination is less likely in the context of a new-onset ischemic stroke due to a ruptured ACoA aneurysm. An elevated Lindegaard ratio is usually associated with vasospasm, which is a common complication following subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). However, vasospasm typically occurs within the first 7-10 days after the initial bleeding, not on day 10. Therefore, an elevated Lindegaard ratio is less likely to be observed on day 10 after the coiling of the aneurysm. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following symptoms is inconsistent with a diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following symptoms is inconsistent with a diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Persistent asymmetry of weakness: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP), or “Guillain-Barre syndrome,” is an autoimmune, areflexic, ascending weakness with mild sensory changes that progresses over a few weeks. It is classically a demyelinating process, although axonal damage may occur in cases of severe demyelination. Predominantly axonal variants also exist (e.g. Miller-Fisher syndrome, acute motor axonal neuropathy). It is often associated with a preceding respiratory infection, gastrointestinal infection, surgery, or vaccination. questions.stem: Which of the following findings on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is suggestive of spontaneous intracranial hypotension?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following findings on brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is suggestive of spontaneous intracranial hypotension?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Flattening of the optic chiasm: Several findings on head MRI can help establish the diagnosis of intracranial hypotension. These include diffuse, non-nodular enhancement of the pachymeninges (without leptomeningeal enhancement); “sagging of the brain” which can result in descent of the cerebellar tonsils, flattening of the anterior pons, obliteration of the basal cisterns and flattening of the optic chiasm; subdural fluid collections; enlargement of the pituitary which can mimic pituitary tumor; engorgement of the cerebral venous sinuses; and decrease in the size of the ventricles. Incorrect Options: Option A - Leptomeningeal Enhancement: Leptomeningeal enhancement refers to the abnormal enhancement of the meninges (the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord) on imaging studies, typically seen as bright areas on contrast-enhanced MRI. While leptomeningeal enhancement can occur in various conditions, such as infections, inflammation, and certain cancers, it is not a specific finding that suggests spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH). Option B - Enlargement of the Basal Cisterns: Enlargement of the basal cisterns is not a typical finding in spontaneous intracranial hypotension. In fact, SIH is characterized by the leakage of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), leading to decreased CSF pressure and resultant brain sagging rather than enlargement of the basal cisterns. Option D - Flattening of the Pituitary: Flattening of the pituitary gland may be seen in cases of intracranial hypotension, but it is not as specific or characteristic as other findings. Spontaneous intracranial hypotension can lead to changes in brain structures, including the downward displacement of the brain ("brain sagging"), which can affect the pituitary gland's position. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 50-year-old female with a history of diabetes is noted to become confused and have trouble standing while on a city bus. The paramedics are called and finds her alert with mild dysarthria and jerking movements of her left arm and left leg. Her finger stick is 100. She arrives as a "stroke code" with vitals of BP 120/80, HR 110, RR 22, Temp 99.0, Sat 98% on RA. You find her alert and conversant with no apparent trauma. Her left arm and left leg are twitching frequently and display greatly increased tone. She has left facial twitching as well and although she has no aphasia, she has mild garbled speech. She has no focal weakness and can lift both arms and legs equally. What should you do for this patient?

Her left arm and left leg are twitching frequently and display greatly increased tone. She has left facial twitching as well and although she has no aphasia, she has mild garbled speech. She has no focal weakness and can lift both arms and legs equally. What should you do for this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: She is having a complicated ischemic stroke and needs a stat CT of the brain and likely should get IV TPA

options.label: C
options.text: She is displaying pseudoseizure behavior and needs a psych consult

options.label: D
options.text: Even though her FS is normal, she may be relatively hypoglycemic and needs a bolus of D-50

questions.solution: Correct Option B - She needs immediate IV lorazepam: She is in epilepsia partialis continua, or a form of status epilepticus with simple partial seizures. In this case the sensorium is clear and there is not generalized movement. The arm and leg are the most commonly affected. As in other seizures , benzodiazepines like lorazepam are the first-line choice to break it. A CT and labs need to be checked in her case since they are new onset, but breaking the seizure and maintaining the airway are what is imperative initially. Incorrect Options: Option A - She is having a complicated ischemic stroke and needs a stat CT of the brain and likely should get IV TPA: A stroke would be characterized by a motor deficit, not by movement. Option C - She is displaying pseudoseizure behavior and needs a psych consult: Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures are not associated with physiological central nervous system dysfunction. Clues that may help with diagnosis include long duration, fluctuating course, asynchronous movements, pelvic thrusting, ictal eye closing or crying, memory recall, side-to-side head or body movements, and absent postictal confusion. Option D - Even though her FS is normal, she may be relatively hypoglycemic and needs a bolus of D-50: Hypoglycemia would present with physiologic signs, including tremor, palpitations, and catecholamine or acetylcholine mediated effects, including anxiety and arousal, sweating, and paresthesias. Other symptoms include cognitive impairment, behavior changes, psychomotor abnormalities, seizure, and coma. Seizures occur at low glucose levels that would be detected. @Neet_pg_bot

Facial sensation is intact and she describes hyperacusis and altered taste on the right side of her tongue. There is no history of rash. The remainder of her exam, including the otoscopic exam, is unremarkable. Laboratory studies show no abnormalities and she is HIV and RPR negative. The strongest evidence exists for which of the following treatments?

options.label: A
options.text: Five grams of IV methylprednisolone over 5 days with eye care/protection

options.label: B
options.text: Eye care/protection alone as steroids and/or antivirals would have no effect on the outcome if they were started this far out from onset

options.label: C

questions.answerText: Oral prednisone for 10 days with eye care/protection
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Oral prednisone for 10 days with eye care/protection: This patient has Bell’s palsy, i.e., an idiopathic unilateral mononeuropathy of cranial nerve VII. Multiple oral steroid regimens (25 mg bid for 10 days, 60 mg for 5 days followed by a taper over 5 days) have proven beneficial (increase rate of recovery and degree of recovery) in RCTs. Incorrect Options: Option A - Five grams of IV methylprednisolone over 5 days with eye care/protection: While corticosteroids (such as methylprednisolone) are commonly used in the treatment of Bell's palsy, the patient's presentation and clinical course are not consistent with Bell's palsy. Bell's palsy typically presents with acute-onset, painless, unilateral facial weakness that reaches its peak within 48 hours and gradually improves over several weeks. In this case, the patient's clinical presentation is more suggestive of a different condition, and IV methylprednisolone is not the most appropriate treatment. Option B - Eye care/protection alone as steroids and/or antivirals would have no effect on the outcome if they were started this far out from onset: This option suggests that treatment with steroids and/or antivirals would not be effective if started one day after symptom onset. However, in cases of acute facial nerve palsy with an incomplete presentation of symptoms within 72 hours, treatment with steroids can be beneficial in improving outcomes. Option D - Valacyclovir for 10 days with eye care/protection: Valacyclovir is an antiviral medication commonly used to treat herpes simplex virus infections, including herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) which can cause facial nerve palsy (Ramsay Hunt syndrome). However, the patient's history does not include a rash, and Ramsay Hunt syndrome is often associated with a vesicular rash in or around the ear canal. Additionally, the presence of hyperacusis and altered taste on the right side of her tongue is not typically seen in Ramsay Hunt syndrome. Therefore, valacyclovir is not the most appropriate treatment in this case. Option E - Oral prednisone and valacyclovir for 10 days with eye care/protection: While combining oral prednisone and valacyclovir is a common approach in the treatment of Ramsay Hunt syndrome, this patient's clinical presentation does not strongly suggest a viral etiology. Additionally, there is no indication of a vesicular rash or other typical findings associated with Ramsay Hunt syndrome. Therefore, this combination of treatments is not the most appropriate option. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of action of vigabatrin?
questions.stemHtml: What is the mechanism of action of vigabatrin?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Inhibition of GABA transaminase: Vigabatrin works through irreversible inhibition of GABA transaminase, decreasing GABA breakdown. Tiagabine inhibits the GABA transporter, leaving more GABA in the extracellular space following synaptic vesicular release. Barbiturates, 1,4-benzodiazepines, and the 1,5-benzodiazepine clobazam directly bind to and potentiate the GABA-A receptor. Incorrect Options: Option B - Sodium channel blocker: Vigabatrin does not directly block sodium channels. Sodium channel blockers are a class of medications that primarily target voltage-gated sodium channels to reduce neuronal excitability and are used in the treatment of epilepsy and other neurological conditions. Option C - Calcium channel blocker: Vigabatrin does not block calcium channels. Calcium channel blockers are a different class of medications that block voltage-gated calcium channels, which can reduce calcium influx into neurons and affect neurotransmitter release. Option D - Inhibition of GABA transporter: Vigabatrin does not inhibit the GABA transporter. GABA transporters are responsible for the reuptake of GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) from the synapse, regulating its concentration in the synaptic cleft. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: It is an inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase inhibitor
questions.solution: Correct Option B - It is an inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase inhibitor: Mycophenolate mofetil is an immunosuppressant agent used as a steroid sparing agent in many neurologic disorders, including neuromyelitis optica. questions.stem: A three-year-old girl is referred to you for evaluation of several months of progressive gait issues. There is no abnormality on the skin examination over her lumbosacral spine, but imaging reveals a low-lying conus medullaris, consistent with tethered cord syndrome. Which of the following is an occult spinal dysraphism associated with tethered cord?
questions.stemHtml:
A three-year-old girl is referred to you for evaluation of several months of progressive gait issues. There is no abnormality on the skin examination over her lumbosacral spine, but imaging reveals a low-lying conus medullaris, consistent with tethered cord syndrome.
Which of the following is an occult spinal dysraphism associated with tethered cord?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Lipomyelomeningocele: Tethered cord syndrome can occur in the setting of both open and occult neural tube defects. Occult spinal dysraphisms have no open defect, but there may be abnormalities of the skin, such as discoloration or a tuft of hair, at the site of the underlying defect. Occult dysraphisms include lipoma, lipomyelomeningocele, dermal sinus, and diastematomyelia (split cord). Open neural tube defects include meningocele (spinal fluid and arachnoid herniate through a dural defect), myelomeningocele (spinal cord tissue, spinal fluid, and arachnoid herniate through defect), hemimyelomeningocele, and myeloschisis (exposed neural tissue without overlying membrane). Incorrect Options: Option A - Hemimyelomeningocele: This is an open neural tube defect where only one half of the spinal cord and its associated structures protrudes through the defect in the vertebral column. It is not associated with occult spinal dysraphism. Option C - Meningocele: This is an open neural tube defect where the spinal fluid and meninges (protective coverings of the spinal cord) herniate through a dural defect. It is not typically associated with tethered cord syndrome. Option D - Myelomeningocele: This is the most severe form of open neural tube defect, where the spinal cord tissue, spinal fluid, and meninges herniate through a defect in the vertebral column. While tethered cord syndrome can develop in individuals with myelomeningocele, the question is specifically asking about an occult spinal dysraphism associated with tethered cord. Myelomeningocele is not an occult condition. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy that requires close monitoring?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy that requires close monitoring?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Renal failure: The adverse effect of acyclovir with the greatest morbidity is crystal-induced nephrotoxicity due to crystallization of the drug within the nephron. Acyclovir has low solubility in urine and therefore it is very important to ensure that patients are not intravascularly depleted as this complication of acyclovir therapy is much higher in patients that are volume contracted. Incorrect Options: Option A - Thrombocytopenia: Thrombocytopenia refers to a low platelet count, which can result in an increased risk of bleeding. Acyclovir is not typically associated with thrombocytopenia as an adverse effect. This option is not a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy and does not require close monitoring specifically for this drug. Option B - Liver Failure: Liver failure involves the severe impairment of liver function. Acyclovir is primarily eliminated by the kidneys, and significant liver toxicity is not a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy. While liver function tests might be monitored in some cases, liver failure is not a typical concern with acyclovir use. Option D - Pancytopenia : Pancytopenia refers to a decrease in all three major blood cell types: red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Acyclovir is not typically associated with pancytopenia. This option is not a common adverse effect of acyclovir therapy and does not require specific monitoring for this drug. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Following resection of a tumor of the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe, what defect would be expected?

questions.solution: Correct Option B - A homonymous right superior quadrantanopia: The left optic radiations serving vision in the right hemifield (in both eyes) originate in the left lateral geniculate nucleus and project to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Fibers serving the superior right quadrant of vision (in both eyes) project through the left temporal lobe in a structure known as the loop of Meyer which passes anteriorly as far as approximately 2.5 cm from the tip of the temporal lobe. Fibers serving the inferior right quadrant of vision (in both eyes) project through the parietal lobe to the primary visual cortex. Lesions of the optic tracts classically cause incongruous (asymmetric between the two eyes) field defects because the visual pathway fibers serving corresponding points in space are not closely approximated. In other words, the more posterior the lesion of the retrochiasmal visual pathways, the more organized the visual pathways fibers are and the more congruous (or symmetric) the visual field defects tend to be. Indeed, occipital lobe lesions tend to cause very congruous homonymous field defects. Lesions of the optic tract anterior to the brachium of the superior colliculus are expected to cause an incongruous contralateral homonymous hemianopic field defect AND a contralateral afferent pupillary defect. The afferent input to the pupillary light reflex, however, separates from the visual pathways just anterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. Therefore, retrogeniculate optic pathway lesions AND pure lateral geniculate nucleus lesions (not involving the optic tract) do not affect pupillary function. Incorrect Options: Option A - A homonymous right inferior quadrantanopia: This option is incorrect because the lesion described in the question involves the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe. Lesions in this area would affect the fibers that carry visual information from the superior right quadrant of the visual field in both eyes. As a result, a homonymous right superior quadrantanopia would be expected, not an inferior quadrantanopia. Option C - A monocular right inferior quadrantanopia in the right eye only: Monocular field defects are not caused by lesions in the brain but rather by abnormalities in the eye itself or along the optic nerve. The lesion described in the question is located in the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe, which is a cerebral region. Therefore, monocular field defects would not be expected. Option D - A monocular right superior quadrantanopia in the right eye only: Similar to option C, monocular field defects are not caused by cerebral lesions. A lesion in the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe would not result in a monocular field defect in the right eye. Option E - A left afferent pupillary defect: Afferent pupillary defects (also known as a Marcus Gunn pupil) are typically caused by lesions affecting the optic nerve or severe retinal disease in the eye. The lesion described in the question is not located along the optic nerve, and it would not cause an afferent pupillary defect. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following interventions/factors has NOT been proven to influence the risk of developing a post-lumbar puncture headache?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following interventions/factors has NOT been proven to influence the risk of developing a post-lumbar puncture headache?

options.label: C
options.text: Replacement of the stylet prior to removal of the needle

options.label: D
options.text: Bevel orientation of a Quincke needle

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Bedrest post-procedure: Despite the common practice of recommending bedrest (“lying flat’) for 30-60 minutes post-procedure, option B is the only factor/intervention of the options listed that hasn’t been shown to have any association with reducing the incidence of post-dural puncture headache (PDPH). Similarly, many of the other factors commonly felt to be associated with an increased risk of a PDPH including patient position, the volume of CSF removed, and the number of attempts made, have also been shown to have no influence on the risk of PDPH. Incorrect Options: Option A - Use of an atraumatic needle: Atraumatic needles, such as Sprotte or Whitacre needles, have a lower risk of causing post-lumbar puncture headaches compared to traditional cutting needles (e.g., Quincke needle). These needles have a rounded tip that separates rather than cuts the dural fibers, reducing the risk of CSF leakage and subsequent headaches. Option C - Replacement of the stylet prior to removal of the needle: Removing the stylet (the inner part of the needle) before removing the needle can create a temporary seal at the puncture site, reducing the risk of CSF leakage and post-lumbar puncture headache. Option D - Bevel orientation of a Quincke needle: The bevel orientation of a Quincke needle (cutting needle) can influence the risk of post-lumbar puncture headache. The bevel orientation should be parallel to the longitudinal axis of the spinal cord, as this reduces the risk of dural fibers being cut and CSF leakage. Option E - Use of a higher gauge (≥ 20 G) needle for the procedure: Smaller gauge needles (e.g., 22 G or 25 G) have been associated with a lower risk of post-lumbar puncture headaches compared to larger gauge needles. The smaller needle size causes less trauma to the dura and reduces the likelihood of CSF leakage. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to the doctor with complaints of missing her menstrual cycle for the past 4 months, despite having regular periods every 28 days with moderate flow. She also reports recurring headaches and difficulty seeing the outer edges of the movie screen without turning her head to either side. Her vitals are within normal limits. Her cranial contrast MRI shows an intrasellar mass. The mass is affecting which of the following?
questions.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman presents to the doctor with complaints of missing her menstrual cycle for the past 4 months, despite having regular periods every 28 days with moderate flow. She also reports recurring headaches and difficulty seeing the outer edges of the movie screen without turning her head to either side. Her vitals are within normal limits. Her cranial contrast MRI shows an intrasellar mass. The mass is affecting which of the following?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Adenohypophysis: This patient's symptoms are consistent with a pituitary adenoma, which is most likely caused by abnormal growth of the adenohypophysis. Adenomas of the pituitary gland are usually due to proliferation of lactotroph cells, leading to hyperprolactinemia and suppression of gonadotropins causing secondary amenorrhea. Bitemporal hemianopsia and headaches may also develop due to compression of the optic chiasm as the adenoma grows. While a large non secreting pituitary adenoma could also explain her symptoms, the absence of other hypopituitarism symptoms makes prolactinoma more likely. Incorrect Options: Option A - Astrocytes: Astrocytomas are associated with rapidly progressive symptoms and typically occur in older individuals moreover this patient's symptoms, including secondary amenorrhea and bitemporal hemianopsia, are more indicative of a pituitary adenoma, which is caused by abnormal growth of cells in the adenohypophysis, not astrocytes. Option C - Arachnoid cap cells: Arachnoid cap cells are not related to the symptoms described in the question stem, which suggest abnormal growth affecting the menstrual cycle and vision. Arachnoid cap cells are a type of cells that make up the arachnoid villi, which play a role in the absorption of cerebrospinal fluid. Option D - Ependymal cells: Ependymomas, which are tumors that arise from ependymal cells, typically cause obstructive hydrocephalus, which can present as recurrent headaches. However, these tumours usually develop during childhood and are not associated with menstrual irregularities or visual disturbances Therefore, it is not likely that abnormal growth of ependymal cells is responsible for the patient's symptoms. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man is brought to the outpatient department because of behavioural changes over the past year. He has been experiencing bouts of depression and hearing voices. He has also developed a tremor in his left hand over the same period that has been worsening lately. Examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly, broad-based gait and a low-frequency tremor that is more prominent in left hand. Sensory examination is unremarkable. Eye examination reveals findings shown in the following photograph. This patient is most likely to have which of the following findings?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old man is brought to the outpatient department because of behavioural changes over the past year. He has been experiencing bouts of depression and hearing voices. He has also developed a tremor in his left hand over the same period that has been worsening lately. Examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly, broad-based gait and a low-frequency tremor that is more prominent in left hand. Sensory examination is unremarkable. Eye examination reveals findings shown in the following photograph. This patient is most likely to have which of the following findings?

options.label: D
options.text: Enlarged ventricles on the CT scan of brain

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Low serum ceruloplasmin levels: The patient's depression, psychosis (hearing voices), tremor and gait disturbance combined with the characteristic eye finding of Keyser-Fleisher rings, suggests Wilson disease. Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene. ATP7B is a copper-transporting protein that is primarily expressed in the liver, where it facilitates the incorporation of copper into ceruloplasmin, a copper-containing protein that is secreted into the blood. Defective ATP7B gene results in defective copper transport and metabolism that leads to copper accumulation in liver leading to cirrhosis. Copper is subsequently deposited in other organs, primarily the basal ganglia in the brain causing neurological dysfunction such as tremors, gait dysfunction, depression and psychosis. Inability of defective ATP7B protein to incorporate copper into apoceruloplasmin leads to low serum ceruloplasmin concentration. Low serum ceruloplasmin is diagnostic for Wilson disease. Incorrect Options: Option A - High serum ferritin: Elevated serum ferritin levels are a common finding in hemochromatosis that can lead to hepatosplenomegaly and signs of liver failure, as well as neurological symptoms if hepatic encephalopathy develops. However, the presence of ascites or peripheral edema would be expected in cases of chronic liver disease. Additionally, hemochromatosis typically presents in patients over 30 years of age and may involve other features, such as skin pigmentation, joint pain, diabetes, and cardiomyopathy and testicular atrophy in males. Option C - Elevated number of CAG repeats: Having an elevated number of CAG repeats on genetic testing is diagnostic of Huntington's disease (HD), which can result in impaired motor abilities such as gait disturbance and tremors. Typical clinical features of HD, including chorea, athetosis, sensory deficits, and autonomic symptoms like sweating and urinary problems, are not present in this patient. Moreover, HD does not affect the liver. Option D - Enlarged ventricles on CT scan of the brain: Enlarged ventricles on brain imaging is indicative of hydrocephalus. Normal pressure hydrocephalus mostly occurs in older individuals and is often associated with difficulty walking. However, since this patient does not exhibit other typical symptoms of NPH like dementia or urinary incontinence, it is less likely to be the underlying cause. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Oxytocin: The anterior pituitary gland is in front of the pituitary gland and is a small pea-sized gland at the base of the brain below the hypothalamus in the Sella turcica. This gland is a part of the endocrine system that controls other endocrine glands' functions. That's why this gland is also called the master gland of the endocrine system. The anterior pituitary is also called adeno hypophysis. It produces thyroid-stimulating, adrenocorticotropic, follicle-stimulating hormone, growth hormone, and luteinizing hormone. Incorrect Options: Option B - Follicle-stimulating hormone: Follicles stimulating hormone stimulates the follicles in the ovary. It also prepares the eggs for ovulation. Option D - Growth hormone: Growth hormone is also called somatotropin hormone / human growth hormone. The anterior lobe of the pituitary gland produces it. It is synthesized and secreted by anterior pituitary cells called somatotrophs. It stimulates the growth of all body tissues, including bone. Growth hormone hypersecretion in children causes gigantism, and in adults causes acromegaly. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - ACTH assay interference: In an SST, blood is first collected for baseline measurement of plasma cortisol and ACTH level. Then, 250 µg of Synacthen is administered intramuscularly, followed by measurement of cortisol levels at 30 and/or 60 minutes post-Synacthen. She reports a history of hyperpigmentation and has a recent diagnosis of autoimmune thyroiditis. On examination, she appears dehydrated, and her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg. Laboratory investigations reveal hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and a low cortisol level. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old female presents to the emergency department with weakness, fatigue, and dizziness. She reports a history of hyperpigmentation and has a recent diagnosis of autoimmune thyroiditis. On examination, she appears dehydrated, and her blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg. Laboratory investigations reveal hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and a low cortisol level. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Addison's disease: The clinical picture of this patient is suggestive of Addison's disease which is the most common cause of Chronic Primary Adrenal Insufficiency in developed nations. Addison's disease is a condition where the adrenal glands do not produce enough cortisol and sometimes aldosterone. The clinical features of Addison's disease include: Fatigue and weakness: One of the most common symptoms of Addison's disease is fatigue, weakness, and malaise. Patients may feel tired even after getting enough rest. Weight loss and decreased appetite: Patients with Addison's disease may experience weight loss and decreased appetite. Hyperpigmentation: This is the darkening of the skin, most commonly seen on the face, neck, and hands. It is caused by an increase in melanin production because melano cortical stimulating hormone (MSH) is produced along with adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) from pro-opiomelanocortin. Hypotension: Low blood pressure due to sodium loss and iso-osmotic water loss is a common feature of Addison's disease. Patients may feel dizzy or faint when they stand up. Salt cravings: Patients may experience salt cravings due to the low aldosterone levels which results in sodium loss. Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea: These symptoms may occur due to the body's inability to regulate electrolyte balance and water. Muscle and joint pain: Patients with Addison's disease may experience muscle and joint pain due to the lack of cortisol in the body. Depression and irritability: Low cortisol levels can also cause emotional changes, such as depression and irritability. Incorrect Options: Option A - Graves’ disease: Graves' disease is an autoimmune disorder causing the thyroid gland to produce excessive thyroid hormone. Symptoms include weight loss, increased appetite, palpitations, rapid heartbeat, tremors, sweating, heat intolerance, goitre, eye problems, skin changes, emotional changes, menstrual irregularities, weakness, and muscle wasting.The clinical features of hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and low cortisol levels in addition to weakness, fatigue, dizziness and hyperpigmentation are suggestive of Addison disease. Option B - Hashimoto thyroiditis: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune disorder affecting the thyroid gland, leading to hypothyroidism. The condition results from the "antithyroid peroxidase and antithyroglobulin antibodies." and damaging the thyroid gland, which results in the gland's inability to produce enough thyroid hormones. This leads to symptoms such as fatigue, weight gain, constipation, depression, and dry skin. However, Addison's disease is an autoimmune disease that primarily affects the adrenal glands, leading to a deficiency of cortisol and aldosterone. Both conditions share some clinical features, such as fatigue and muscle weakness, but the main different clinical features are: Hyperpigmentation of the skin, especially in sun-exposed areas Salt cravings Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) Nausea and vomiting Dizziness or lightheadedness upon standing up (orthostatic hypotension) Option D - Cushing disease: Cushing's disease is a condition caused by the overproduction of cortisol hormone by the pituitary gland. The excess cortisol can cause a wide range of symptoms, including weight gain, high blood pressure, muscle weakness, and increased risk of infections. While Cushing’s disease and Addison’s disease share some similar features like fatigue, weakness, changes in weight, mood swings and increased risk of infection, there are some key differences for example, Cushing disease can cause symptoms such as high blood pressure, a round "moon" face, and a buffalo hump on the back, while Addison's disease can cause symptoms such as low blood pressure, hyperpigmentation of the skin, and salt cravings. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - High cortisol and low ACTH: Cushing syndrome involves the excess of all adrenal hormones. It is diagnosed by: Demonstration of high cortisol level Serum ACTH levels Dexamethasone suppression test Salivary cortisol 24-hour urinary-free cortisol Radiologic imaging. The outpatient initial screening test is 24-hour urinary-free cortisol. The best initial diagnostic test is an overnight dexamethasone suppression test followed by a 1 mg loading dose. To localise the lesion, a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is carried out to differentiate between pituitary adenoma and ectopic source. If ACTH is low and cortisol is high, there is either an adrenal adenoma or exogenous glucocorticoid intake. However, if ACTH is high and cortisol is low, then there is either pituitary adenoma or an ectopic source that secretes ACTH, such as small cell cancer of the lung. If the cortisol levels are suppressed, followed by a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test, the cause is a pituitary adenoma. Contrarily, if no suppression has occurred, the cause is an ectopic source of ACTH. Incorrect Options: Option B - High cortisol and high ACTH: If ACTH is high and cortisol is also high, there is either pituitary adenoma (Cushing’s disease) or an ectopic source that secretes ACTH, such as small cell cancer of the lung. Option D - Decreased urinary free cortisol: Increased urinary-free cortisol is present in Cushing syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Contrarily, if no suppression has occurred, the cause is an ectopic source of ACTH.

  • Option C - Hyperkalemia and hyponatremia: In Cushing syndrome, there is an excess aldosterone secretion that results in hypernatremia and hypokalemia.
  • Option D - Decreased urinary free cortisol: Increased urinary-free cortisol is present in Cushing syndrome.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old female presents to the endocrinology clinic complaining of increased irritability, sensitivity to heat, weight loss, and vibrations. Laboratory tests show an increase in free T4 and a decrease in TSH. Which mechanisms are most likely responsible for the observed changes in this patient's thyroid gland physiology?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old female presents to the endocrinology clinic complaining of increased irritability, sensitivity to heat, weight loss, and vibrations. Laboratory tests show an increase in free T4 and a decrease in TSH. Which mechanisms are most likely responsible for the observed changes in this patient's thyroid gland physiology?

options.label: C
options.text: Ingestion of excessive amounts of dietary iodine

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Autoantibodies against thyroid-stimulating hormone receptors: The patient's clinical features of increased irritability, sensitivity to heat, weight loss, and vibrations suggest hyperthyroidism , which is characterised by increased thyroid hormone production. Autoantibodies against thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH ) receptors are key in developing Graves' disease, the most common cause of hyperthyroidism. These autoantibodies, known as thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI), bind to and activate the TSH receptors on thyroid follicular cells, mimicking the action of TSH. As a result, the thyroid gland produces and releases excessive amounts of thyroid hormones (T3 and T4), leading to the symptoms associated with hyperthyroidism. The binding of TSI to TSH receptors triggers a cascade of events, including increased iodine uptake, thyroid hormone synthesis, and thyroid gland growth. The elevated levels of thyroid hormones in the bloodstream then exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary gland, suppressing the release of thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) and TSH. This feedback loop results in the decreased TSH levels typically observed in patients with Graves' disease. The clinical manifestations of hyperthyroidism due to Graves' disease include heat intolerance, increased irritability, weight loss, palpitations , and fatigue. Additionally, patients may develop Graves' ophthalmopathy , characterised by exophthalmos (protrusion of the eyeballs), periorbital oedema, and diplopia (double vision). Incorrect Options: Option B - Increased production of thyroxine-binding globulin: Increased thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) production can lead to elevated total T4 levels but would not affect free T4 levels or cause the symptoms described in the scenario. TBG binds to thyroid hormones, reducing their free (biologically active) concentrations. Changes in TBG levels usually have minimal effect on thyroid function. Option C - Ingestion of excessive amounts of dietary iodine: While excessive iodine intake can cause thyroid dysfunction, it typically results in hypothyroidism (reduced thyroid function) rather than the hyperthyroidism observed in this case. The Wolff-Chaikoff effect describes a transient decrease in thyroid hormone synthesis due to high iodine intake, leading to decreased thyroid function. Option D - Dysfunction of the parathyroid glands: Dysfunction of the parathyroid glands can result in abnormal calcium metabolism but does not directly affect thyroid gland physiology. The parathyroid glands produce parathyroid hormone (PTH), which regulates calcium homeostasis, and are not involved in producing or regulating thyroid hormones. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presents with complaints of headache, lethargy, and nausea for the last 20 days after an episode of pneumonia. On examination, there is no remarkable finding but laboratory investigations reveal a serum sodium level of 128mEq/L, serum osmolality 270mOsm/kg, urinary sodium level of 44mEq/L, and urinary osmolality 110mOsm/kg. What is the first-line treatment for a mild case of this disease?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male presents with complaints of headache, lethargy, and nausea for the last 20 days after an episode of pneumonia. On examination, there is no remarkable finding but laboratory investigations reveal a serum sodium level of 128mEq/L, serum osmolality 270mOsm/kg, urinary sodium level of 44mEq/L, and urinary osmolality 110mOsm/kg. What is the first-line treatment for a mild case of this disease?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Fluid restriction: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH) is characterized by excess ADH secretion which causes excess water absorption from the kidney and results in concentrated urine SIADH is diagnosed by Serum sodium lower than 135mEq/L Serum osmolality lower than 275mOsm/kg Urine sodium higher than 40mEq/L Urine osmolality higher than 100mOsm/kg With normal blood pressure and euvolemia and no other causes of hyponatremia Pulmonary diseases like pneumonia, asthma, acute respiratory failure, and pneumothorax can cause SIADH due to unknown mechanism Clinical manifestations are due to decreased serum osmolality due to ADH-mediated water retention and secondary solute loss which causes cerebral edema The 1st line treatment for a patient with mild symptoms is the fluid restriction The daily water intake is restricted to less than 800ml only This restricted intake of water decreases free water in the body and increases serum osmolality and improves symptoms Incorrect Options: Option B - Salt tablets: If the 1st line treatment of water restriction is not helpful and hyponatremia is persistent then sodium chloride in the form of salt tablets can be given to correct hyponatremia Salt tablets cause effective and rapid response than water restriction Option C - Salt tablets with furosemide: Salt tablets (sodium chloride) can be used with furosemide (a loop diuretic) as it decreases the urine concentration and helps the excretion of water This is not a first-line treatment and is used after water restriction Option D - Hypertonic saline infusion: The hypertonic saline infusion will rapidly increase the serum sodium levels and will cause osmotic demyelination syndrome In a patient with mild symptoms of hyponatremia rapid correction with hypertonic saline is not recommended @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option A - Fluid restriction:

  • Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH) is characterized by excess ADH secretion which causes excess water absorption from the kidney and results in concentrated urine
  • SIADH is diagnosed by
    • Serum sodium lower than 135mEq/L
    • Serum osmolality lower than 275mOsm/kg
    • Urine sodium higher than 40mEq/L
    • Urine osmolality higher than 100mOsm/kg
    • With normal blood pressure and euvolemia and no other causes of hyponatremia
  • Pulmonary diseases like pneumonia, asthma, acute respiratory failure, and pneumothorax can cause SIADH due to unknown mechanism
  • Clinical manifestations are due to decreased serum osmolality due to ADH-mediated water retention and secondary solute loss which causes cerebral edema
  • The 1st line treatment for a patient with mild symptoms is the fluid restriction
  • The daily water intake is restricted to less than 800ml only
  • This restricted intake of water decreases free water in the body and increases serum osmolality and improves symptoms

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Salt tablets:

  • If the 1st line treatment of water restriction is not helpful and hyponatremia is persistent then sodium chloride in the form of salt tablets can be given to correct hyponatremia
  • Salt tablets cause effective and rapid response than water restriction

Option C - Salt tablets with furosemide:

  • Salt tablets (sodium chloride) can be used with furosemide (a loop diuretic) as it decreases the urine concentration and helps the excretion of water
  • This is not a first-line treatment and is used after water restriction

Option D - Hypertonic saline infusion:

  • The hypertonic saline infusion will rapidly increase the serum sodium levels and will cause osmotic demyelination syndrome
  • In a patient with mild symptoms of hyponatremia rapid correction with hypertonic saline is not recommended

questions.stem: A second-year medical student learns about the regulation and function of prolactin in his endocrinology lecture. Which of the following dopaminergic pathway is involved in the secretion of prolactin?
questions.stemHtml: A second-year medical student learns about the regulation and function of prolactin in his endocrinology lecture. Which of the following dopaminergic pathway is involved in the secretion of prolactin?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Tuberoinfundibular: Prolactin is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland . Its secretion is inhibited by the production of dopamine by the tuberoinfundibular pathway of the hypothalamus . Decreased activity of this pathway results in increased production of prolactin. Thyroid-releasing hormone (TRH) can also stimulate the production of prolactin in conditions like primary or secondary hypothyroidism. Prolactin can inhibit its own secretion by increasing dopamine production from the hypothalamus. Functions of prolactin include: Stimulation of milk production Inhibition of ovulation (females) Inhibition of spermatogenesis (males) Dopamine agonists (cabergoline) are used to treat conditions in which prolactin excess (prolactinoma). Drugs like antipsychotics and antidepressants can decrease dopamine production and can result in an increase in prolactin levels. Incorrect Options: Option A - Mesocortical: Decreased activity of the mesocortical pathway results in negative symptoms like anergia and apathy. It is affected minimally by antipsychotics. Option B - Mesolimbic: Increased activity of the mesolimbic pathway results in positive symptoms like delusions and hallucinations. Antipsychotics have a marked effect on these pathways. Option C - Nigrostriatal: Decreased activity of nigrostriatal pathways results in extrapyramidal symptoms like dystonia and parkinsonism. It is notably affected by movement disorders. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Hypophosphatemia, hypercalcemia: Hypophosphatemia and hypercalcemia are the main biochemical findings observed in hyperparathyroidism. The parathyroid hormone is the primary hormone that regulates calcium levels in the body. Hyper parathyroid hormone causes the elevation of calcium levels and decreases the phosphate level . Parathyroid hormone acts on the different parts of the body, which causes the serum calcium levels to increase and serum phosphate levels to decrease in the following ways: Bones It stimulates the osteoblasts at a low serum level, thus building bone. At a higher level, it stimulates osteoclastic activity, thus enhancing bone resorption. Kidney Stimulates 1 alpha-hydroxylase activity . Activates vitamin D. Intestine Increases absorption of both calcium and phosphate. Factors affecting PTH level: Low magnesium elevates PTH Very low magnesium decreases PTH Increased phosphate increases PTH secretion. Low calcium stimulates PTH secretion. Incorrect Options: Option B - Hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia with hyperuricemia: Tumour lysis syndrome occurs when cancer cells break down rapidly, releasing large amounts of intracellular contents into the bloodstream. Lab findings show: Increased potassium levels above 25% from the baseline. Calcium levels al s o decreased by about 25% from the baseline The level of uric acid may also be increased. Option C - Normal phosphate, hypercalcemia: High calcium levels and normal phosphate are seen in the high calcitonin. Option D - Hypernatremia, hypokalemia: Hypernatremia and hypokalemia are seen in Adrenal insufficiency due to a lack of aldosterone and glucocorticoids. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Hyper parathyroid hormone causes the elevation of calcium levels and decreases the phosphate level.
  • Parathyroid hormone acts on the different parts of the body, which causes the serum calcium levels to increase and serum phosphate levels to decrease in the following ways:
    • Bones
      • It stimulates the osteoblasts at a low serum level, thus building bone.
      • At a higher level, it stimulates osteoclastic activity, thus enhancing bone resorption.
    • Kidney
      • Stimulates 1 alpha-hydroxylase activity.
      • Activates vitamin D.
    • Intestine
      • Increases absorption of both calcium and phosphate.
  • Factors affecting PTH level:
    • Low magnesium elevates PTH
    • Very low magnesium decreases PTH
    • Increased phosphate increases PTH secretion.
    • Low calcium stimulates PTH secretion.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia with hyperuricemia:

  • Tumour lysis syndrome occurs when cancer cells break down rapidly, releasing large amounts of intracellular contents into the bloodstream.
  • Lab findings show:
    • Increased potassium levels above 25% from the baseline.
    • Calcium levels also decreased by about 25% from the baseline
    • The level of uric acid may also be increased.

Option C - Normal phosphate, hypercalcemia: 

  • High calcium levels and normal phosphate are seen in the high calcitonin.

Option D - Hypernatremia, hypokalemia: 

  • Hypernatremia and hypokalemia are seen in Adrenal insufficiency due to a lack of aldosterone and glucocorticoids.

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Surgical bypass of the annular ring: Annular pancreas is a congenital abnormality of the pancreas defined by a ring of pancreatic tissue encapsulating the descending portion of the duodenum, most likely due to incomplete rotation of the embryologic ventral pancreatic bud. Since it is usually asymptomatic, the incidence is unknown, but it appears to occur rarely. It is characterized as complete or incomplete and classified into subtypes based upon the drainage of the annular duct. Symptoms may occur as early as the neonatal period, but age of onset is determined by severity of obstruction. Typically, adults present between the ages of 20 and 50 with chronic abdominal pain, early satiety, nausea, and vomiting. Performance of cholangiopancreatogram allows delineation of the structure of the annular duct and accessory pancreatic duct. In patients who are symptomatic, treatment is surgery to relieve gastric outlet or duodenal obstruction by a bypass of the annulus. Incorrect Options: Option A - Pancreaticoduodenectomy: Pancreaticoduodenectomy or Whipple procedure may be indicated in patients with obstructive pancreatic duct stones and chronic pancreatitis or in those who have a potentially malignant periampullary lesion. Diabetes mellitus is the systemic disorder most commonly associated with gastroparesis. Studies based on the general population report UGI symptoms in up to 18% of patients, but patients with DM studied in tertiary care centers have demonstrated delayed gastric emptying in 55-60% of cases. In the general population, gastroparesis has a cumulative incidence of 0.2% in controls compared to 5% in patients with type I DM and 1% in type 2 DM. Incorrect Options: Option A - Parkinson disease: Gastroparesis can be caused by enteric nervous system dysfunction in patients with Parkinson’s disease, but it is not the most common cause. Option B - Primary dysautonomia: Primary dysautonomias are not as common. Other conditions that affect extrinsic neural control include multiple sclerosis, brainstem stroke or tumor, and amyloid neuropathy. Diabetes also affects extrinsic neural control of the UGI tract. Option D - Post-viral dysautonomia: Some patients with gastroparesis have sudden onset after viral prodromes. Prior infection with Norwalk virus and rotavirus have also been associated with gastroparesis. Incorrect Options: Option A - He should continue to undergo surveillance endoscopy to see if this develops into carcinoma: This option is incorrect because dysplasia in Barrett's esophagus is considered a precancerous condition. When dysplasia is identified, it indicates an increased risk of developing esophageal carcinoma (cancer). As such, continued surveillance is not the appropriate course of action. Intervention is required to prevent the progression to carcinoma. Option B - He should undergo radiofrequency ablation therapy: This option is incorrect because radiofrequency ablation (RFA) therapy is typically used for the treatment of Barrett's esophagus with low-grade dysplasia or high-grade dysplasia that does not involve any visible cancer (carcinoma in situ). In this case, the patient has dysplasia on several histologic specimens, which may indicate a more advanced stage than what RFA can address. Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) or other treatments might be more suitable. Option C - He should undergo photodynamic therapy: This option is incorrect because photodynamic therapy (PDT) is used for treating high-grade dysplasia or early-stage esophageal carcinoma that is limited to the superficial layers of the esophagus (also known as intramucosal carcinoma). In this case, the patient has dysplasia but no visible mucosal irregularities, which suggests that PDT may not be the most appropriate treatment. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Follow-up ultrasound in 6 months: Gallbladder polyps are commonly found on routine abdominal ultrasound. Management of gallbladder polyps is based on available evidence of clinical characteristics that suggest increased risk for malignancy. Patient risk factors for malignant polyps include age over 60, presence of gallstones, and primary sclerosing cholangitis. Polyp characteristics associated with higher risk are sessile morphology, size over 6 mm, and solitary polyps. Patients with polyps who have symptoms that are suggestive of biliary colic should generally undergo cholecystectomy. This patient has non-specific symptoms and a polyp that is 5 mm. Although there is no consensus on the time to follow-up, some experts recommend an initial follow-up at 3 months for polyps 6-9 mm in asymptomatic patients without signs of malignancy. questions.stem: Which of the following would not be associated with a false-positive or false-negative gastric emptying study?

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Elevated hemoglobin A1c levels: While hyperglycemia at the time of the gastric emptying study can be associated with delayed gastric emptying and a false-positive gastric emptying study, a history of diabetes or an elevated hemoglobin A1c level with a normal blood glucose at the time of the study will not be associated with a false-positive test. Anticholinergic agents such as benztropine will also be associated with a false-positive study. However, domperidone, which is used to stimulate gastric motility (but is not approved for use in the United States), can lead to a false-negative gastric emptying study. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hyperglycemia: Hyperglycemia refers to high blood sugar levels, which can be associated with diabetes. Option C - Domperidone: Domperidone is a medication used to treat nausea and vomiting. It works by increasing the movement or contractions of the stomach and intestines. If someone is taking domperidone during the gastric emptying study, it might influence the test results by affecting gastric motility. It could lead to false-negative results, where the study may show normal or faster gastric emptying due to the effects of the medication. Option D - Benztropine: Benztropine is an anticholinergic medication used to treat certain movement disorders and side effects of antipsychotic medications. questions.stem: Which of the following parasitic infections is usually associated with occult blood in stool?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following parasitic infections is usually associated with occult blood in stool?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Strongyloides: TRUE: Occult blood in stool is associated with hookworm or Strongyloides infection. Strongyloides stercoralis enters the human host when skin contacts the larvae through infected soil usually contaminated with feces. The parasite can live for up to 5 years in humans, eventually burrowing into the mucosa of the duodenum as adults. Eggs produced by the adult female pass in the feces. Eosinophilia points to a parasite infection. The adult worm migrates to the small bowel and can cause duodenitis, leading to epigastric pain that is aggravated by food ingestion. Patients complain of diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. Pulmonary manifestations can include wheezing, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Lipid infusions are associated with an increased rate of infections in critically ill patients: Although a short period of nutritional deprivation may be tolerated, physiologic function and nutritional status are affected by significant deprivation over 1-2 weeks. In critically ill patients, nutritional support should be initiated relatively as early as 24-48 hours after admission, as it may improve outcomes. Option D - The absence of bowel sounds is a contraindication to enteral feeding : The only contraindication to enteral feeding is high bowel obstruction. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Anti-reflux surgery has been shown to improve symptoms in patients with regurgitation: Multiple studies have shown that while anti-reflux surgery does help with symptoms in certain patients, it does not alter an individual’s risk for esophageal cancer. Endoscopic anti-reflux procedures including radiofrequency augmentation of the lower esophageal sphincter and endoscopic suturing of the sphincter have not been proven to result in long-term symptom control. Studies have shown that at 3 years after the procedures, patients continued to need medical therapy or a fundoplication procedure. Anti-reflux surgery is contraindicated in patients with metaplasia or dysplasia since it can affect treatment options in case of progression to cancer. Finally, anti-reflux surgery is associated with worsening of dysphagia in some patients; thus, there is no guarantee that her dysphagia will resolve. questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of tumour suppressor genes?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a characteristic of tumour suppressor genes?

options.label: A
options.text: The mutant allele is often inherited through the germ line

options.label: B
options.text: The somatic mutation does not contribute to cancer

options.label: C
options.text: The inherited form of the mutant allele does not commonly have a tissue preference

options.label: D
options.text: The mutant allele acts in a dominant fashion

questions.answerText: The mutant allele is often inherited through the germ line
questions.solution: Correct Option A - The mutant allele is often inherited through the germ line Unlike oncogenes, tumour suppressor genes are commonly inherited through the germ line. The only known example of an oncogene being inherited due to a dominant germline mutation in a proto-oncogene is the RET oncogene, which leads to multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2). Oncogenes act as gain of function mutations and require only one mutation, while tumour suppressor genes generally function as loss of function mutations and require two mutations. Incorrect Options: Option B - The somatic mutation does not contribute to cancer: Somatic mutations in tumor suppressor genes can indeed contribute to cancer development. Somatic mutations are acquired during an individual's lifetime and occur in non-germline cells, such as somatic cells of the body. These mutations can lead to the loss of function of tumor suppressor genes, which, in turn, can result in uncontrolled cell growth and the development of cancer. Inactivation of tumor suppressor genes in somatic cells is a common event in various cancers. Option C - The inherited form of the mutant allele does not commonly have a tissue preference: The inherited form of the mutant allele in some tumor suppressor genes can indeed show a tissue preference or predisposition for specific types of cancer. For example, individuals with germline mutations in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 tumor suppressor genes have a higher risk of developing breast and ovarian cancers. Similarly, individuals with germline mutations in the APC gene have an increased risk of developing colorectal cancer. Option D - The mutant allele acts in a dominant fashion: Tumor suppressor genes typically act in a recessive fashion at the cellular level. This means that both copies (alleles) of the tumor suppressor gene must be inactivated or lost to contribute to the development of cancer. Inherited germline mutations in tumor suppressor genes increase the risk of cancer development, but it usually requires a second "hit" or somatic mutation in the remaining allele to cause complete loss of function and lead to cancer. The loss of both alleles is usually required for the manifestation of malignancy at the cellular level, even though the inheritance pattern at the organismal level may be autosomal dominant. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 67-year-old female with a h/o mantle cell lymphoma, treated with BR + filgrastim, and then subsequently with R-CHOP plus PEG-filgrastim for progressive disease, now presents to your clinic, 4 years later with a diagnoses of t-MDS. Which is the most likely culprit?
questions.stemHtml: A 67-year-old female with a h/o mantle cell lymphoma, treated with BR + filgrastim, and then subsequently with R-CHOP plus PEG-filgrastim for progressive disease, now presents to your clinic, 4 years later with a diagnoses of t-MDS. Which is the most likely culprit?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Filgrastim Therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS) and acute myeloid leukemia (t-AML) are known complications of chemotherapy and radiation therapy used to treat various malignancies, including non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). Filgrastim is a granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) that is commonly used to reduce the risk of neutropenia (low white blood cell count) in patients receiving myelosuppressive chemotherapy, such as the regimens used to treat mantle cell lymphoma (e.g., BR and R-CHOP). While filgrastim can help prevent severe neutropenia, it has been associated with an increased risk of t-MDS and t-AML, especially when used in combination with certain chemotherapeutic agents. The SEER (Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results) database review mentioned in the answer supports the association between filgrastim and t-MDS in patients with NHL. The review found a 3.7% incidence of t-MDS/AML in NHL patients exposed to filgrastim but not PEG-filgrastim. Incorrect Options: Option A - Rituximab: Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody commonly used in the treatment of mantle cell lymphoma and other B-cell lymphomas. It is not directly associated with an increased risk of t-MDS. Option B - Bendamustine: Bendamustine is an alkylating agent used in the treatment of various lymphomas, including mantle cell lymphoma. While it can be associated with some adverse effects, it is not specifically linked to an increased risk of t-MDS. Option D - PEG-filgrastim: PEG-filgrastim is a long-acting form of filgrastim that is used to reduce the duration of neutropenia after chemotherapy. While t-MDS risk may be lower with PEG-filgrastim compared to regular filgrastim, it is still associated with some risk. The SEER database review mentioned in the correct answer did not specifically address the association of PEG-filgrastim with t-MDS, so it is not clear if PEG-filgrastim carries a similar risk. However, it is still important to consider the possibility of t-MDS in any patient who has received prior chemotherapy and presents with myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukemia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: For which FIGO stages of ovarian cancer is surgery an appropriate front-line treatment?
questions.stemHtml: For which FIGO stages of ovarian cancer is surgery an appropriate front-line treatment?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- I, II, III, IV: FIGO staging for ovarian cancer is as follows: Stage I: Tumour limited to the ovaries Stage II: Tumour involves one or both ovaries with pelvic extension and/or implants Stage III: Tumour involves one or both ovaries with spread to the peritoneum outside the pelvis or retroperitoneal lymph node metastases Stage IV: Extra-peritoneal distant metastases In patients with FIGO stage III disease, optimal debulking (no macroscopic gross residual disease) improves overall survival outcomes This is reflected in the current NCCN guidelines which recommend surgical debulking for patients with any stage disease who are medically operable and for whom optimal cytoreduction is the likely outcome. Incorrect Options: Option A - I: Surgery is indeed an appropriate front-line treatment for stage I ovarian cancer. In early-stage ovarian cancer, surgery aims to remove the tumor and any involved tissue to achieve complete debulking. Option B - I, II: This option includes stages I and II. Surgery is generally considered the primary treatment approach for both of these early stages of ovarian cancer. Option C - I, II, III: This option includes stages I, II, and III. Surgery is an appropriate front-line treatment for these stages. In cases of stage III ovarian cancer, surgery may involve more extensive procedures to achieve optimal debulking. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option D- I, II, III, IV:

  • FIGO staging for ovarian cancer is as follows:
    • Stage I: Tumour limited to the ovaries
    • Stage II: Tumour involves one or both ovaries with pelvic extension and/or implants
    • Stage III: Tumour involves one or both ovaries with spread to the peritoneum outside the pelvis or retroperitoneal lymph node metastases
    • Stage IV: Extra-peritoneal distant metastases
  • In patients with FIGO stage III disease, optimal debulking (no macroscopic gross residual disease) improves overall survival outcomes
  • This is reflected in the current NCCN guidelines which recommend surgical debulking for patients with any stage disease who are medically operable and for whom optimal cytoreduction is the likely outcome.

Option C - I, II, III: This option includes stages I, II, and III. Surgery is an appropriate front-line treatment for these stages. In cases of stage III ovarian cancer, surgery may involve more extensive procedures to achieve optimal debulking.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of cellular senescence?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a feature of cellular senescence?

options.label: A
options.text: Loss of ability to secrete tumorigenic growth factors

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Permanent cell cycle arrest Cellular senescence is irreversible cell cycle arrest. Cellular senescence is a programmed cellular response to significant stress. Cells that are in senescence are unable to divide and there are no known physiologic signals that can stimulate senescent cells to proliferate. However, they remain metabolically active and can continue to secrete mitogens that may promote growth of nearby tumour cells. The cellular membrane remains intact and they do not necessarily undergo apoptosis or necrosis. Senescence occurs when cells experience a potentially "oncogenic stress" that could result in progression to malignancy. Thus, it is a mechanism by which cells attempt to prevent carcinogenesis. Examples of causes include depletion of chromosomal telomeres, accumulated DNA damage, or lack of nutrients. It is dependent on activation of the p53 and Rb proteins, which lead to chromatin modifications preventing necessary gene expression for the G1 to S cell cycle transition. Incorrect Options: Option A - Loss of ability to secrete tumorigenic growth factors: This statement is incorrect. Senescent cells can still secrete various factors, including growth factors, cytokines, and proteases, collectively known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Some of these factors may have tumor-promoting effects, which is one of the reasons why senescent cells are implicated in aging and cancer. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Serum iron 15 μg/dL, TIBC 420 μg/dL, serum ferritin 10 μg/L, percent saturation 7%: This set of lab values is most consistent with iron deficiency anemia caused by chronic blood loss, such as from a bleeding duodenal ulcer. Serum Iron: Low serum iron levels are expected in iron deficiency anemia because the body's iron stores are depleted due to chronic bleeding. TIBC (Total Iron Binding Capacity): Elevated TIBC indicates that the body is trying to compensate for low iron levels by increasing its capacity to bind and transport iron. Serum Ferritin: Ferritin is an indicator of the body's iron stores. In this case, the low ferritin level reflects depleted iron stores. Percent Saturation: The percent saturation of transferrin (serum iron/TIBC x 100) is also low due to the insufficient amount of iron available to bind with transferrin. Incorrect Options: Option B - Serum Iron 100 μg/dL, TIBC 420 μg/dL, Serum Ferritin 10 μg/L, Percent Saturation 7%: While the low ferritin and percent saturation are consistent with iron deficiency, a serum iron level of 100 μg/dL is not indicative of iron deficiency anemia, especially considering the low ferritin level and low percent saturation. Iron levels are expected to be low in iron deficiency anemia. Option C - Serum Iron 15 μg/dL, TIBC 420 μg/dL, Serum Ferritin 100 μg/L, Percent Saturation 40%: A serum ferritin level of 100 μg/L is not consistent with iron deficiency anemia. Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and can be elevated in various inflammatory conditions, which would not fit the clinical presentation of this patient with suspected bleeding. Option D - Serum Iron 100 μg/dL, TIBC 325 μg/dL, Serum Ferritin 100 μg/L, Percent Saturation 40%: Similar to the second choice, the high serum iron level is not consistent with iron deficiency anemia due to chronic bleeding. questions.stem: A 60-year-old male recently diagnosed with AML (M4 variant) is on standard induction therapy with cytarabine (seven day continuous infusion) + an anthracycline (given days 1-3) (7+3 therapy). The patient is paraplegic and is very concerned about developing diarrhea and mucositis during induction therapy. Which of the following medications has been demonstrated to reduce the incidence of severe diarrhea in patients undergoing induction therapy for AML?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male recently diagnosed with AML (M4 variant) is on standard induction therapy with cytarabine (seven day continuous infusion) + an anthracycline (given days 1-3) (7+3 therapy). The patient is paraplegic and is very concerned about developing diarrhea and mucositis during induction therapy. Which of the following medications has been demonstrated to reduce the incidence of severe diarrhea in patients undergoing induction therapy for AML?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Palifermin: Palifermin is a medication that belongs to the class of keratinocyte growth factors. It plays a crucial role in promoting the growth and repair of epithelial tissues, including the gastrointestinal (GI) mucosa. Patients undergoing intensive chemotherapy regimens, such as those used in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) induction therapy, are at risk of developing severe mucositis and diarrhea due to the damage chemotherapy inflicts on rapidly dividing cells, including those lining the GI tract. Palifermin has been demonstrated to be effective in reducing the incidence of severe diarrhea in patients undergoing induction therapy for AML. A study (Bradstock et al., Br J Haematol 2014) investigated the use of palifermin as prophylaxis against gastrointestinal toxicity after AML induction therapy. The study found that patients who received palifermin had a statistically significant lower rate of grades 3 and 4 gastrointestinal adverse events, primarily due to a reduction in severe diarrhea. While the primary endpoint of reducing grade 3 and 4 oral mucositis was not statistically significant, the study did show evidence of reduced rates of higher grades of oral mucositis in the palifermin arm as well. Incorrect Options: Option A- Zofran (ondansetron): Zofran is an antiemetic medication commonly used to prevent nausea and vomiting associated with chemotherapy. While it helps with nausea and vomiting, it doesn't directly address the issue of severe diarrhea or mucositis in patients undergoing intensive chemotherapy. Option B- Compazine (prochlorperazine): Compazine is also an antiemetic medication that can help manage nausea and vomiting. Like Zofran, it doesn't specifically target mucositis or diarrhea. Option C- Imodium (loperamide): Imodium is an antidiarrheal medication that can be used to manage diarrhea. While it can be helpful in controlling diarrhea symptoms, it doesn't address the underlying issue of mucositis or prevent severe diarrhea in patients undergoing intensive chemotherapy. @Neet_pg_bot

She was given type O blood, with some units that were Rh positive. 2 months later she consults you to discuss future pregnancy planning. Her current partner is Rh positive. What is the ideal mode of management?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old female, Rh negative, after an RTA had required more than 20 units of blood. She was given type O blood, with some units that were Rh positive. 2 months later she consults you to discuss future pregnancy planning. Her current partner is Rh positive. What is the ideal mode of management?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Give a dose of anti- Rh immunoglobulin

options.label: C

questions.answerText: Give a dose of anti- Rh immunoglobulin
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Give a dose of anti- Rh immunoglobulin: In Rh-negative women who have been exposed to Rh-positive blood, such as through transfusion or pregnancy with an Rh-positive fetus, there is a risk of developing Rh sensitization. Rh sensitization can lead to the production of antibodies against Rh-positive blood, which can be a significant concern in future pregnancies. To prevent this, a dose of anti-Rh immunoglobulin (Rhogam) is administered to the Rh-negative woman. This immunoglobulin binds to any Rh-positive blood cells that might have entered her bloodstream, preventing her immune system from reacting to them and thus reducing the risk of sensitization. This is particularly important when the woman is planning future pregnancies with an Rh-positive partner to prevent the development of HDN in the newborn. Incorrect Options: Option A - Check serum for anti-IgG Rh anti-body: Checking serum for anti-IgG Rh antibody is not the ideal approach in this situation. The goal is to prevent Rh sensitization, and waiting for the development of antibodies could lead to complications in future pregnancies. Option C - Confirm the Rh status of the partner: Confirming the Rh status of the partner is important, but regardless of the partner's Rh status, if the woman is Rh-negative and has been exposed to Rh-positive blood, administration of anti-Rh immunoglobulin is recommended to prevent sensitization. Option D - No further intervention: No further intervention is not appropriate in this case. Rh sensitization can lead to hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) in future pregnancies, which can cause severe anemia and other complications in the baby. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: B
