questions.answerText: Pre-storage leukoreduction of the blood product
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Pre-storage leukoreduction of the blood product: The clinical history, signs and symptoms are consistent with a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction, which can occur with any blood product (although this reaction most commonly occurs with RBCs and platelets). Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions occur due to the generation and accumulation of cytokines in stored blood products. Therefore, the risk of having a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction positively correlates with increased number of leukocytes in the blood product, as well as the age of the blood product itself. Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions are clinically characterized by the onset of fever (typically 1-2 degrees Celsius increase in body temperature from baseline), chills or rigors that occur 1-6 hours after initiation of the transfusion. A febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction is a diagnosis of exclusion, after other causes of fever in association with a transfusion (such as hemolysis and sepsis) have been ruled out. The primary strategy to prevent the onset of a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction is prestorage leukoreduction of the blood product (answer choice B), which entails passing the cellular blood products through a filter during collection (apheresis) or shortly after collection to remove most of the leukocytes. In addition to reducing the risk of a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction, leukoreduction also decreases the risk of graft rejection in transplant recipients and immune-mediated platelet destruction by minimizing exposure to HLA antigens present on transfused, donor leukocytes. Similarly, leukoreduction also decreases the risk of transfusion-transmitted CMV, as the CMV virus resides within white blood cells. Incorrect Options: Option A - Irradiation of the blood product: Irradiation of blood products causes DNA crosslinks, preventing the replication of lymphocytes without significantly damaging the function of RBCs, platelets or granulocytes. Irradiation of blood products prevents transfusion-associated GVHD in immunosuppressed individuals with deficient cellular immunity and in those receiving blood transfusions from a directed donor (first degree relative donor). Option C - Washing of the blood product: Washing of blood products (answer choice C) removes the plasma component of RBC and platelets. However, there is no role for washing to prevent the onset of febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions. Option D - Prophylactic administration of acetaminophen prior to initiation of the transfusion: Prophylactic treatment with acetaminophen (answer choice D) is incorrect, as this is not beneficial for preventing febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions. In a double-blinded randomized controlled trial, 315 hematology-oncology patients were randomized to receive either acetaminophen (500 mg) plus diphenhydramine (25 mg) versus placebo 30 minutes prior to transfusion, and monitored for 4 hours. There was no significant difference in the pretreatment and placebo groups with respect to transfusion reactions (1.4 versus 1.5 reactions per 100 transfusions, respectively) (Kennedy et al. Transfusion 2008). Similarly, another review of 6 studies also found no demonstrable benefit of pre-medication with acetaminophen and diphenhydramine to prevent transfusion reactions @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male notices haematuria of 3 days duration. O/E- icteric and mild abdominal diffuse tenderness, vitals are stable. Lab evaluation demonstrates anaemia, reticulocytosis, decreased haptoglobin, and elevated LDH and bilirubin. To further evaluate his condition, you proceed with flow-cytometry which demonstrates an absence of CD55 and CD59. Which bone marrow disorder is most closely related to the patient's underlying condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male notices haematuria of 3 days duration. O/E- icteric and mild abdominal diffuse tenderness, vitals are stable. Lab evaluation demonstrates anaemia, reticulocytosis, decreased haptoglobin, and elevated LDH and bilirubin. To further evaluate his condition, you proceed with flow-cytometry which demonstrates an absence of CD55 and CD59. Which bone marrow disorder is most closely related to the patient's underlying condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Aplastic anaemia: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) is an unusual condition with patients typically presenting in their 30s. The genetic underpinning of this condition is an acquired somatic mutation of the PIGA gene (Phosphatidylinositol Glycan class A) on the X chromosome. The protein product of the PIGA gene is involved in the creation of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor which serves to attach cell surface proteins to the cell membrane. Without the GPI anchor for protein attachment, these cells are prone to both intravascular haemolysis (lack of CD59) and extravascular haemolysis (lack of CD55). Clinical symptoms typically include erectile dysfunction, abdominal pain, (these smooth muscle symptoms are thought to be secondary to a decreased amount of nitric oxide caused by free haemoglobin during haemolysis) profound fatigue, and haematuria (see intravascular haemolysis above) especially during night-time hours. Thrombosis (large abdominal vein) is common in this patient population as free haemoglobin is associated with a pro-thrombotic milieu. Laboratory abnormalities include: high levels of LDH, low levels of haptoglobin, unbound haemoglobin in the urine, anaemia, reticulocytosis, with a negative direct ant globin test (Coombs test). The diagnosis can be confirmed using flow cytometry. PNH and aplastic anaemia are often found in tandem (this occurs in greater than 50% of cases). Although not completely understood, the underlying mechanism appears to be immune escape by PNH cells and subsequent proliferation in the setting on aplastic anaemia Incorrect Options: Option A - Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML): CML is a type of cancer that starts in certain blood-forming cells of the bone marrow. It is characterized by a specific genetic abnormality in the cancer cells, the Philadelphia chromosome. CML would not explain the absence of CD55 and CD59 as seen in PNH. Option B - Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS): MDS refers to a group of diverse bone marrow disorders in which the bone marrow does not produce enough healthy blood cells. While MDS might cause anaemia and other blood-related symptoms, the absence of CD55 and CD59, as well as the patient's overall clinical picture, are more consistent with PNH than with MDS. Option D - Fanconi's anaemia: Fanconi's anaemia is a rare inherited bone marrow failure syndrome that is characterized by physical abnormalities, bone marrow failure, and a higher risk of cancer. The genetic basis and clinical presentation differ from those of PNH. The described findings and clinical picture, such as the absence of CD55 and CD59, are not typical for Fanconi's anaemia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman presents to your OPD with a history of repeated blood transfusions from childhood. She doesn’t remember the final diagnosis, but recalls that she has never been sick enough to need admission. Initial screening labs in clinic demonstrate the following: WBC : 6.1 x 10^3/uL Hgb: 8.6 g/dL MCV: 69 fL RBC : 6.5 x 10^6/uL Platelet Count: 342 x 10^3/uL Ferritin: 1,362 ng/mL TSH: 2.5 mIU/L Na : 142 mmol/L K : 4.9 mmol/L Cl : 105 mmol/L HCO3-: 25 mmol/L BUN : 15 mg/dL Creatinine: 0.9 mg/dL Total Bilirubin: 2.1 mg/dL AST : 22 U/L ALT : 34 U/L Alkaline Phosphatase: 50 U/L Albumin: 4 g/dL Haptoglobin: Undetectable LDH : 400 U/L Her peripheral smear shows target cells and hypochromic microcytic anaemia. According to the above labs and the patient's presentation, what do you recommend as the next step in management?

questions.solution: Correct Option D - MRI liver: The patient's presentation and laboratory findings suggest that she likely has thalassemia intermedia or a relatively benign form of thalassemia major. Thalassemias are inherited disorders of hemoglobin synthesis that result in microcytic, hypochromic anemia due to reduced production of one or more globin chains. MRI of the liver is a non-invasive method used to assess the degree of systemic iron deposition in patients with thalassemia. Elevated serum ferritin levels suggest iron overload, and MRI can provide valuable information about iron concentration within the liver. Monitoring for iron overload is important to prevent potential complications associated with excess iron accumulation, including liver damage. Incorrect Options: Option A - Bone marrow biopsy: A bone marrow biopsy is not typically necessary for the diagnosis or management of patients with thalassemia. Thalassemia is characterized by abnormal hemoglobin production, and the diagnosis can often be confirmed through peripheral blood tests, hemoglobin electrophoresis, and other relevant lab investigations. Option B - Peripheral blood flow cytometry: Peripheral blood flow cytometry is not necessary in this case. Flow cytometry is used to analyze and characterize different cell populations, often focusing on immune cells or hematological malignancies, but it's not indicated for the diagnosis of thalassemia. Option C - Liver biopsy: A liver biopsy could be used to diagnose iron overload, but it's invasive and not necessary when other non-invasive methods are available. Iron overload is a concern in patients with thalassemia due to both increased iron absorption and potential blood transfusions, but there are better methods, such as MRI, to assess iron levels in the liver. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 27-year-old G1P0 female who is currently 25 weeks pregnant presents to the emergency department with vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. Her vital signs are significant for a blood pressure of 88/52 mm of hg and a heart rate of 122/min. A bedside ultrasound reveals a placental abruption. Laboratory studies indicate a hemoglobin level of 6.7 g/dL, platelets of 70,000/mcL, a prothrombin time (PT) of 33 seconds, a partial thromboplastin time (PTT) of 74 seconds, a creatinine level of 3.4 mg/dL, and an indirect bilirubin of 2.5. A peripheral blood smear reveals many schistocytes. Which of the following is responsible for these abnormalities?
questions.stemHtml: A 27-year-old G1P0 female who is currently 25 weeks pregnant presents to the emergency department with vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. Her vital signs are significant for a blood pressure of 88/52 mm of hg and a heart rate of 122/min. A bedside ultrasound reveals a placental abruption. Laboratory studies indicate a hemoglobin level of 6.7 g/dL, platelets of 70,000/mcL, a prothrombin time (PT) of 33 seconds, a partial thromboplastin time (PTT) of 74 seconds, a creatinine level of 3.4 mg/dL, and an indirect bilirubin of 2.5. A peripheral blood smear reveals many schistocytes. Which of the following is responsible for these abnormalities?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Release of tissue factor: This patient developed disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) due to a placental abruption . The microangiopathic hemolytic anemia of DIC results from the widespread activation of clotting due to tissue factor activation. The release of tissue factor induces a cascade of intravascular clot formation. These clots contain both platelets and coagulation factors, and patients experience both a hyper and hypocoagulable state. Microvascular fibrin deposition causes ischemic multiorgan dysfunction. Laboratory studies will demonstrate low platelets, low hemoglobin levels (with the presence of schistocytes), and low fibrinogen. Elevations occur in PT/PTT, fibrin degradation products (D-dimers), indirect bilirubin, and creatinine. DIC can accompany a wide range of pathologies including sepsis, trauma, pancreatitis, malignancy, nephrotic syndrome, severe burns, and obstetric complications. Management of DIC is supportive and includes transfusions of packed red blood cells, platelets, fresh frozen plasma, and cryoprecipitate as warranted. The underlying disease must be addressed. Incorrect Options: Option A - Formation of anti-GpIIb/IIIa antibodies: The formation of auto-antibodies to anti-GpIIb/IIIa occurs in immune thrombocytopenia (ITP ). ITP typically results in much lower platelet counts and does not lead to anemia or abnormal coagulation times. Flares may occur during pregnancy in patients who have pre-existing ITP or other autoimmune diseases. Treatment consists of steroids or intravenous immune globulin (IVIG). Option B - Deficiency of ADAMTS13: ADAMTS13 deficiency is the mechanism of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP ). ADAMTS 13 degrades von Willebrand multimers. When it is deficient, these multimers increase, leading to increased platelet adhesion, aggregation, and subsequently thrombus formation. Similar to DIC, these thrombi cause microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. However, since the clots result from the sole consumption of platelets and not coagulation factors, the prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times are normal. Treatment consists of plasma exchange. Option C - Release of bacterial toxin: Hemolytic uremic syndrome also involves microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. This condition is caused by a shiga-like toxin t hat is released by enterohemorrhagic E. coli. Bloody diarrhea is typical and young children are affected disproportionately. Like TTP, the thrombi are composed solely of platelets. Treatment is supportive. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - 52 year old G4P4 female with her son as the platelet donor: Generally, multiparous women are more likely than men or nulliparous women to develop alloimmunization to platelets. Furthermore, receiving a transfusion with her son as the donor puts her at an even higher risk, as she may have developed antibodies to the child's father's HLA antigens during her pregnancy. Most cases (~2/3) of platelet refactoriness are NOT due to alloimmunization. However, in cases that are, most are due to antibodies that are created in response to HLA class I antigens on leukocytes or platelets. These antibodies can exist in multiparous women due to maternal-fetal HLA incompatibility during pregnancy. Fetal HLA class I antigens inherited from the father are recognized by the mother as foreign. Multiple pregnancies will put the patient at a higher risk of developing such antibodies. Furthermore, receiving a transfusion with her son as the donor greatly increases the risk of re-presenting HLA class I antigens to antibodies which she has developed.Platelet alloimmunization can also occur in patients who have received multiple transfusions or due to antibodies to platelet specific antigens (human platelet antigens). Incorrect Options: Option A - 52-year-old G0P0 female with her husband as the platelet donor: Alloimmunization to platelet transfusion is more common in multiparous women, as they are exposed to foreign HLA antigens during pregnancy. In this case, the patient has not been pregnant before (G0P0), which lowers her likelihood of developing alloantibodies. Additionally, her husband's HLA antigens are less likely to trigger an immune response compared to antigens from her own offspring. Option B - 52 -year-old G0P0 female with a random platelet donor: This patient is also a nulliparous woman (G0P0), reducing her risk of developing alloimmunization to platelet transfusion. In this case, the donor is random, meaning the donor's HLA antigens are not specifically associated with those of her offspring. questions.solution: Correct Option C- Measurement of glomerular filtration rate (GFR): The diagnosis of CKD involves a combination of clinical assessment, laboratory tests, and imaging studies. The following are the steps involved in the diagnosis of CKD: Assessment of risk factors: The first step in the diagnosis of CKD is to assess the patient's risk factors, including age, family history, medical history, and lifestyle factors. Evaluation of symptoms: The next step is to evaluate the patient's symptoms, such as fatigue, weakness, loss of appetite, and swelling in the legs and ankles. Measurement of kidney function: Kidney function is typically measured using a blood test that measures the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and the level of creatinine in the blood. Urine tests: Urine tests are also used to diagnose CKD. The presence of protein or blood in the urine can indicate kidney damage. Imaging studies: Imaging studies such as ultrasound, CT scan, or MRI may be used to look for structural abnormalities in the kidneys. Biopsy: In some cases, a kidney biopsy may be necessary to diagnose CKD. A small sample of kidney tissue is removed and examined under a microscope to look for signs of damage or disease. Incorrect Options: Option A- Renal biopsy: Renal biopsy is not the initial step in the diagnosis of CKD, as renal biopsy is an invasive procedure and is usually reserved for cases in which the diagnosis is unclear or for patients with suspected glomerulonephritis. questions.stem: A 44-year-old man came to the clinic with complaints of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency for the last 3 days. He has had hypertension and diabetes mellitus for the last eight years. Urine culture reveals Proteus mirabilis and has been adequately treated. He has had recurrent episodes of urinary tract infections in the last two years. This patient is most likely to develop which of the following conditions?
questions.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man came to the clinic with complaints of dysuria, urinary frequency, and urgency for the last 3 days. He has had hypertension and diabetes mellitus for the last eight years. Urine culture reveals Proteus mirabilis and has been adequately treated. He has had recurrent episodes of urinary tract infections in the last two years. This patient is most likely to develop which of the following conditions?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Struvite stones. Struvite stones (magnesium ammonium phosphate) are formed due to upper urinary tract infections from urease-positive organisms, i.e. Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella pneumonia, Enterobacter, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Urease produced by these organisms converts urea into ammonia. Increased alkalinization of the urine due to raised ammonia levels leads to the precipitation of ammonium magnesium phosphate salt resulting in stone formation. These stones are large and are usually present in the renal pelvis and calyces. "Staghorn" refers to a branched kidney stone occupying the renal pelvis and at least one calyceal system. Struvite stones usually present with urinary tract infections or hematuria, not as acute renal pain. The mainstay of the treatment is treating the underlying infection, hydration, acidification of urine and ultimately, surgical removal of the stone like PCNL and ESWL. Incorrect options: Option A: Cystine stones These stones are moderately radio-opaque and are formed due to impaired proximal renal tubular absorption of dibasic amino acids which are cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine, not due to infections, and are formed in acidified urine. Usually begins in childhood. Can form staghorn calculi. Sodium cyanide nitroprusside test ⊕. Treatment: low sodium diet, alkalinization of urine, chelating agents (eg, tiopronin, penicillamine) if refractory. Option B: Calcium oxalate stones Calcium stones most common (80%); calcium oxalate more common than calcium phosphate stones. Can result from ethylene glycol (antifreeze) ingestion, vitamin C overuse, hypocitraturia (usually associated with decreased urine pH), malabsorption (eg, Crohn disease). Option D: Uric acid stones These stones are most common type of radiolucent renal stone and are formed due to increased uric acid levels in the blood and urine, either due to increased intake or to the production of uric acid inside the body. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents with edema, fatigue, and frothy urine. Blood tests show hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Urinalysis shows proteinuria, with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 5. A kidney biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane and spike-like projections on silver stain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old female presents with edema, fatigue, and frothy urine. Blood tests show hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Urinalysis shows proteinuria, with urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 5. A kidney biopsy shows diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane and spike-like projections on silver stain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Membranous nephropathy: Membranous nephropathy is a type of glomerulonephritis that affects the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) of the kidneys, leading to proteinuria and often nephrotic syndrome. It is a relatively common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, with an estimated incidence of 2-10 cases per million per year. The diagnosis of membranous nephropathy is typically made based on a combination of clinical presentation, laboratory tests, and kidney biopsy findings. The clinical presentation usually includes edema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, and hyperlipidemia. Urine tests will show significant proteinuria, often with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of greater than 3-4. Blood tests may show hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. Kidney biopsy is necessary to confirm the diagnosis of membranous nephropathy and to distinguish it from other types of glomerulonephritis. The biopsy findings in membranous nephropathy typically show diffuse thickening of the GBM, with subepithelial immune complex deposits that can be seen on electron microscopy. The deposits may appear as spike-like projections or as granular deposits. The glomeruli may also show evidence of mesangial expansion and interstitial fibrosis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is classified into three subtypes based on the location of the immune deposits within the glomeruli. These types include: Type I MPGN Type II MPGN (also known as dense deposit disease) Type III MPGN (also known as immune complex-mediated MPGN) Type I MPGN is the most common subtype and is characterized by subendothelial immune deposits, while type II MPGN is characterized by dense intramembranous deposits of complement component C3. Type III MPGN is rare and is characterized by subepithelial or intramembranous immune deposits. Option C - Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a type of acute nephritic syndrome that occurs as a result of an immune response to a group A streptococcal infection, typically a pharyngeal or skin infection. PSGN is more common in children than in adults, and it typically resolves on its own within a few weeks to months. On biopsy, PSGN is characterized by diffuse endocapillary proliferation. There may also be neutrophil infiltration, fibrinoid necrosis, and a "lumpy-bumpy" appearance of the glomeruli due to the deposition of immune complexes. Immunofluorescence staining may show granular deposits of immunoglobulin G (IgG), immunoglobulin M (IgM), and C3 along the glomerular basement membrane. Option D - Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is a type of glomerulonephritis that progresses rapidly, usually over days to weeks, and can lead to severe renal impairment or even renal failure. There are several types of RPGN, biopsy findings show crescentic glomerulonephritis with other findings specific to each type. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 1-year-old girl is brought to you with a 2-days history of high-grade fever and crying while passing urine. Two months ago, she was treated for pyelonephritis with cefixime. Her temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F), and her pulse is 118/min. On examination, there is tenderness at the costovertebral junction. The urine dipstick shows leukocyte esterase; urinalysis shows WBCs. A micturating cystourethrogram shows vesicoureteral reflux. Without treatment, he Is likely to develop which of the following complication in the future?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Chronic kidney disease The history of recurrent pyelonephritis in children is linked to vesicoureteral reflux, confirmed by a micturating cystourethrogram. Chronic kidney disease is a long-standing complication of untreated VUR Vesicoureteral reflux: The retrograde urine flow from the bladder into the ureter and kidneys is known as vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). Before developing a urinary tract infection, patients with VUR typically show no symptoms. The symptoms include fever, dysuria, burning micturition (crying while passing urine), urgency, and flank pain. The UTI is frequently recurrent. Complications Chronic kidney disease; long-standing untreated VUR can lead to the development of chronic kidney disease Chronic retrograde flow of urine caused by VUR increases the pressure within the lumen of the nephron. It dilates the renal calyces, leading to compression of the surrounding blood vessels, causing a decrease in the blood flow through these vessels and hypoperfusion of the kidneys. Ischemia of the renal parenchyma leads to atrophic changes in the kidney, which Is responsible for replacing the renal parenchyma with scar tissue. If VUR is left untreated, it will lead to progressive destruction of the nephron and renal scarring that ends up in the development of CKD. Secondly, chronic pyelonephritis also accelerates the progression of scarring and the development of CKD Other complications of VUR include urosepsis, perinephric abscess, and renal scarring. Vesicoureteral reflux: 

  • The retrograde urine flow from the bladder into the ureter and kidneys is known as vesicoureteral reflux (VUR).
  • Before developing a urinary tract infection, patients with VUR typically show no symptoms. The symptoms include fever, dysuria, burning micturition (crying while passing urine), urgency, and flank pain. The UTI is frequently recurrent.

  • Chronic kidney disease; long-standing untreated VUR can lead to the development of chronic kidney disease
    • Chronic retrograde flow of urine caused by VUR increases the pressure within the lumen of the nephron. It dilates the renal calyces, leading to compression of the surrounding blood vessels, causing a decrease in the blood flow through these vessels and hypoperfusion of the kidneys.
    • Ischemia of the renal parenchyma leads to atrophic changes in the kidney, which Is responsible for replacing the renal parenchyma with scar tissue. If VUR is left untreated, it will lead to progressive destruction of the nephron and renal scarring that ends up in the development of CKD.

    • Other complications of VUR include urosepsis, perinephric abscess, and renal scarring.

  • VUR does not increase the risk of the development of renal cell carcinoma
  • Von-Hippel Lindau syndrome is responsible for the development of RCC in children

Option C: Ureteric stricture 

  • Vesicoureteral reflux leads to the development of hydroureter and hydronephrosis due to the retrograde flow of urine in the ureters and renal pelvis that elevates the pressure in the ureters and renal pelvis 
  • It does not give rise to ureteric stricture formation

  • VUR does not increase the risk of nephrotic syndrome as the nephrotic syndrome is caused by diseases that damage the glomeruli
  • The nephrotic syndrome manifests with proteinuria, body swellings, and hyperlipidemia

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Initiation of renal replacement therapy (RRT): The treatment of severe acute kidney injury (AKI) involves aggressive management of the underlying cause and supportive care to maintain vital organ function. The initial management of AKI includes hemodynamic stabilization, which is achieved through fluid resuscitation and correction of electrolyte abnormalities. In cases of severe AKI, renal replacement therapy (RRT) may be required to replace the kidney's filtration function. There are two types of RRT: haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis. Hemodialysis is the most common form of RRT, which involves the use of an external machine to filter blood through a semipermeable membrane. Peritoneal dialysis, on the other hand, involves the installation of a special solution into the abdominal cavity, which helps to remove excess fluid and waste products from the body. In addition to RRT, other treatments may be necessary to manage the underlying cause of AKI. For example, antibiotics may be given for infections, and medication adjustments may be made for patients with drug-induced AKI. Close monitoring and management of complications, such as electrolyte imbalances, acidosis, and fluid overload, are also essential components of the treatment of severe AKI. Incorrect Options: Option A- Administration of a high dose of a loop diuretic: Loop diuretics are commonly used in the management of fluid overload in AKI. However, in cases of severe AKI, where the kidney function is severely compromised, loop diuretics may not be effective in reducing fluid overload. Moreover, high doses of loop diuretics may lead to electrolyte imbalances, such as hypokalemia and hyponatremia. Option C- Empiric antibiotic therapy: Antibiotic therapy is not a standard treatment option for AKI. Although AKI can be caused by infections, such as pyelonephritis or sepsis, antibiotics are only used in these cases. Empiric antibiotic therapy can lead to the development of antibiotic resistance and adverse effects, such as diarrhoea and allergic reactions. Option D- Intravenous infusion of 0.9% saline: Intravenous infusion of 0.9% saline is used in the management of hypovolemia and dehydration. However, in cases of AKI, the administration of 0.9% saline can lead to volume overload and exacerbate the condition. The use of intravenous fluids is guided by the patient's fluid status and electrolyte levels, and excessive fluid administration should be avoided. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D: Abdominal CT scan or MRI Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is a rare genetic disorder (autosomal dominant) due to mutations in the VHL gene on chromosome 3p26-p25. Individuals with VHL disease are at risk of hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytomas, and clear cell renal cell carcinoma. Individuals with von Hippel-Lindau disease have an increased risk of developing renal cell carcinoma (RCC), which is the most common tumor associated with this genetic disorder. Therefore, imaging studies such as a CT scan or MRI of the abdomen may be ordered to screen for RCC in this patient. Other imaging studies, such as retinal exams and brain MRIs, may also be considered depending on the patient's clinical presentation and symptoms. There is currently no cure for VHL disease, but treatment options are available to manage the symptoms and complications of the condition. These may include surgery, radiation therapy, medications, and regular monitoring to detect and manage any new tumors. Incorrect options: Option A: Bone density scan This is a test that uses X-rays to measure bone mineral density and assess the risk of osteoporosis and fractures. Bone density scans are not typically indicated for the screening of tumors associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease. Option B: Echocardiogram Echocardiograms are not typically indicated for the screening of tumors associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease, as the syndrome is primarily associated with tumours in the kidneys, adrenal glands, pancreas, and central nervous system. Option C: Colonoscopy Colonoscopies are not typically indicated for the screening of tumours associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease, as the syndrome is not typically associated with an increased risk of colon cancer. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man visits his doctor for a check-up. He had an emergency heart catheterization three weeks ago due to a myocardial infarction. He was hospitalized for longer than anticipated due to decreased kidney function. The patient claims that his symptoms have improved considerably since then. He is now urinating considerably more than he was before the procedure. His serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL, and his blood urea nitrogen concentration is 20 mg/dL. Which of the following problems is this patient more likely to experience?
questions.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man visits his doctor for a check-up. He had an emergency heart catheterization three weeks ago due to a myocardial infarction. He was hospitalized for longer than anticipated due to decreased kidney function. The patient claims that his symptoms have improved considerably since then. He is now urinating considerably more than he was before the procedure. His serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL, and his blood urea nitrogen concentration is 20 mg/dL. Which of the following problems is this patient more likely to experience?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Hypokalemia About two weeks after the initial event, acute kidney injury (AKI) patients typically recover full glomerular filtration function. However, tubular reabsorption is still impaired, leading to increased urine production and subsequent polyuria. Several electrolytes, such as potassium, sodium, and magnesium, that are typically reabsorbed by the tubules, are lost during the polyuric recovery period of AKI. Incorrect options: Option B: Hypernatremia This patient is in the polyuric recovery stage of AKI three weeks after exposure to contrast and is more at risk for hyponatremia than hypernatremia. Patients experience several electrolyte losses during this time, including sodium, which is typically reabsorbed by the tubules. Option C: Hyporeninemia Patients with AKI in the polyuric recovery phase are at risk for volume depletion, characterized by a decline in GFR and salt delivery to the distal nephrons and the subsequent release of renin. As a result, this patient would produce more renin. Option D: Metabolic alkalosis This patient's polyuric recovery phase of AKI has been present for three weeks following contrast exposure. Patients are at risk for metabolic acidosis rather than alkalosis during this time because they cannot excrete H+ ions and regenerate bicarbonate (both functions of the tubule system). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option: C Create free radicals to damage bacterial DNA Nitrofurantoin is used for antibiotic prophylaxis in children >3 months with vesicoureteral reflux who have shown an acute reaction following the administration of sulfonamide antibiotics. Nitrofurantoin is reduced to reactive intermediates by bacterial nitro reductases, which then attack ribosomal proteins, DNA and other molecules within the cell. Adverse effects GI (gastrointestinal) upset Hemolytic anemia in patients with glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency Peripheral neuropathy Liver toxicity Hepatitis Pulmonary fibrosis Contraindications Neonates< 01 month G6PD deficiency Pregnant women at term ( 38 to 42 weeks) During labor and delivery Impaired renal function( creatinine clearance < 60mL/min) Incorrect options: Option A: Inhibit cell wall synthesis by blocking peptidoglycan crosslinking Ampicillin and amoxicillin are less effective as prophylactic agents and are usually reserved for infants < 2 months of age. Option B: Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a folic acid synthesis inhibitor and is used as a drug of choice for prophylactics management in children > 3 months with VUR; however, this patient has shown an allergic reaction following administration of a sulfa-containing antibiotic; therefore the use of TMP-SMZ is contraindicated. Option D: Inhibit 30S subunit of bacterial ribosomes Tetracyclines bind with the 30S subunit of ribosomes and inhibit bacterial protein synthesis. They are not recommended to be used for prophylaxis in children with VUR. They also cause tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia. @Neet_pg_bot

Adverse effects

  • GI (gastrointestinal) upset
  • Hemolytic anemia in patients with glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency
  • Peripheral neuropathy
  • Liver toxicity
  • Hepatitis
  • Pulmonary fibrosis

Contraindications

  • Neonates< 01 month
  • G6PD deficiency
  • Pregnant women at term ( 38 to 42 weeks)
  • During labor and delivery
  • Impaired renal function( creatinine clearance < 60mL/min)

Incorrect options:

Option A: Inhibit cell wall synthesis by blocking peptidoglycan crosslinking

  • Ampicillin and amoxicillin are less effective as prophylactic agents and are usually reserved for infants < 2 months of age.

Option B: Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis

  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a folic acid synthesis inhibitor and is used as a drug of choice for prophylactics management in children > 3 months with VUR; however, this patient has shown an allergic reaction following administration of a sulfa-containing antibiotic; therefore the use of TMP-SMZ is contraindicated.

Option D: Inhibit 30S subunit of bacterial ribosomes

  • Tetracyclines bind with the 30S subunit of ribosomes and inhibit bacterial protein synthesis. They are not recommended to be used for prophylaxis in children with VUR.
  • They also cause tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician due to a one-month history of weight gain and facial oedema. Her blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, her pulse is 80/min, and her examination shows 2+ ankle oedema. Urine analysis shows 3+ proteinuria and fatty casts. Which of the following is most likely the cause of her proteinuria?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician due to a one-month history of weight gain and facial oedema. Her blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, her pulse is 80/min, and her examination shows 2+ ankle oedema. Urine analysis shows 3+ proteinuria and fatty casts. Which of the following is most likely the cause of her proteinuria?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Glomerular proteinuria The patient, in this case, has nephrotic syndrome. Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome characterized by the following: Proteinuria (> 3-3.5 g/day - most important manifestation) Hypoalbuminemia Edema Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria The basic pathology is the altered permeability of the glomerular membrane for proteins. Diseases most commonly causing nephrotic syndrome are: Minimal change disease (in children) Membranous glomerulopathy (adults) Mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis Proteinuria is excessive protein excretion in the urine, generally greater than 150 mg daily in adults. Proteinuria can be associated with high serum creatinine levels, elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) or evidence of systemic illness (e.g., fever, rash, vasculitis). Glomerular proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormalities in the glomerular filtration barrier in the kidneys. The glomerular filtration barrier is a complex structure comprising three layers: the fenestrated endothelium, the basement membrane, and the podocytes. This barrier is responsible for filtering out waste products and excess fluid from the blood while preventing larger molecules, such as proteins, from entering the urine. Glomerular proteinuria can occur when there is damage or disruption to any of these layers, which can lead to the passage of protein into the urine. It results from the effacement of epithelial cell foot processes and altered glomerular permeability with an increased filtration fraction of normal plasma proteins, as in diabetic nephropathy. Protein electrophoresis will have a pattern exhibiting a large albumin spike indicative of the increased permeability of albumin across the damaged GBM. Incorrect options: Option A: Functional proteinuria Functional proteinuria is not due to any underlying disease or medical condition but a functional body response to certain stressors. This type of proteinuria is usually benign and self-limiting and does not require any specific treatment. Functional proteinuria can be caused by a variety of factors, including: Exercise Fever Emotional stress Dehydration Functional proteinuria is a benign process resulting from acute illness, exercise, and "orthostatic proteinuria." Orthostatic proteinuria usually causes protein excretion of less than 1 g/day. It occurs only during the daytime and is associated with an upright posture. This patient has a history of nephrotic syndrome, so functional proteinuria is unlikely. Option C: Tubular proteinuria Tubular proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormalities in the reabsorption of proteins by the tubular cells in the kidneys. Normally, the kidney tubular cells reabsorb small amounts of protein that pass through the glomeruli and into the filtrate. However, in tubular proteinuria, there is a defect in the tubular cells that impairs their ability to reabsorb proteins, leading to increased protein levels in the urine. It occurs as the reabsorption of normally filtered proteins in the proximal tubule is defective. It occurs due to a variety of causes: Acute tubular necrosis Toxic injury (lead, aminoglycosides and certain antiretrovirals), Drug-induced interstitial nephritis Hereditary metabolic disorders (Wilson disease and Fanconi syndrome). Option D: Overload proteinuria Overload proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormal blood proteins that exceed the renal tubules' reabsorptive capacity. In this type of proteinuria, the excess protein is not due to a defect in the glomerular filtration barrier or tubular reabsorption but rather due to an excess of abnormal proteins that the renal tubules cannot properly reabsorb. Overload proteinuria can result from: Overproduction of circulating, filterable plasma proteins (monoclonal gammopathies), such as Bence Jones proteins associated with plasma cell myeloma (formerly multiple myeloma). Amyloidosis: Amyloidosis is a condition in which abnormal proteins build up in various tissues in the body, including the kidneys, and can lead to overflow proteinuria. Sickle cell disease: Sickle cell disease can cause the breakdown of red blood cells, releasing hemoglobin into the blood and urine, leading to overflow proteinuria. Fabry disease: It is a genetic disorder in which a buildup of a specific type of fat in the body can produce abnormal proteins that can be excreted in the urine, leading to overflow proteinuria. Protein electrophoresis from the serum or urine will exhibit a discrete protein peak. Other examples of overload proteinuria include myoglobinuria in rhabdomyolysis and hemoglobinuria in hemolysis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with end-stage renal disease due to polycystic kidney disease has presented to the physician's clinic. He has been on hemodialysis for the past six months and has a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus type 2. Which of the following is the most appropriate indication for renal transplantation in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Symptomatic uremia: Patients with end-stage renal disease (Irreversible kidney dysfunction with eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m2) often experience a range of symptoms due to the accumulation of waste products and the loss of kidney function. These symptoms, collectively known as uremia, can include fatigue, nausea, vomiting, pericarditis, peripheral neuropathy pleuritis, lethargy, confusion, seizures, somnolence, coma, and pruritus. There is increased bleeding risk and infection. Renal transplantation is a well-established treatment for uremia , as it can restore kidney function and alleviate these symptoms. Incorrect Options: Option A- Uncontrolled hypertension: Although hypertension is a common complication of end-stage renal disease, it does not indicate renal transplantation. Hypertension can usually be managed with medications and lifestyle changes, and kidney transplantation may not necessarily improve hypertension control. Option B- Poor glycemic control: While diabetes mellitus is a common cause of end-stage renal disease, poor glycemic control does not indicate renal transplantation. Transplantation may improve glucose control in some patients, but other treatments can also achieve glycemic control . Option D- Polycystic kidney disease: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is a genetic disorder that causes cysts to form in the kidneys, leading to progressive kidney damage and end-stage renal disease. PKD is a common indication for renal transplantation, as it is usually irreversible and can only be treated by replacing the damaged kidneys with a healthy donor kidney. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and confusion. Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis reveals respiratory acidosis. Which of the following structures in the kidney is responsible for regulating acid-base balance?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man presents to the emergency department with shortness of breath and confusion. Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis reveals respiratory acidosis. Which of the following structures in the kidney is responsible for regulating acid-base balance?
questions.solution: Option C- Proximal tubule: The kidneys play a key role in regulating the acid-base balance of the body by removing excess acid or base from the blood. The proximal tubule is the primary site of acid-base regulation in the kidney, where bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) are reabsorbed from the filtrate and returned to the bloodstream. Bicarbonate ions are important for buffering acids in the blood and maintaining a pH that is compatible with normal bodily functions. When there is an excess of acid in the blood, such as in the case of respiratory acidosis, the kidneys respond by increasing the reabsorption of bicarbonate ions in the proximal tubule, which helps to neutralise the excess acid and restore the acid-base balance of the body. This process is regulated by several mechanisms, including the action of carbonic anhydrase enzymes in the proximal tubule, which catalyse the conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O) into carbonic acid (H2CO3), which dissociates into bicarbonate ions and hydrogen ions (H+). The hydrogen ions are secreted into the filtrate in exchange for the reabsorption of bicarbonate ions, which are then returned to the bloodstream to help buffer excess acid. Therefore, option C is correct because the proximal tubule is responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. Incorrect Options: Option A- Glomerulus: The glomerulus is responsible for filtering blood and removing waste products from the bloodstream, but it is not directly involved in regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. The glomerulus is a network of capillaries in the renal corpuscle that is responsible for filtering blood and producing a filtrate that contains water, electrolytes, and waste products. The filtrate produced by the glomerulus is then modified as it passes through the renal tubules, where various substances are reabsorbed back into the bloodstream or secreted into the urine. While the glomerulus is not directly involved in acid-base regulation, it does play a role in maintaining the electrolyte balance of the body by filtering out excess sodium and other electrolytes from the blood. Therefore, option A is incorrect because the glomerulus is not responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. Option B- Bowman's capsule: Bowman's capsule is the cup-shaped structure that surrounds the glomerulus in the renal corpuscle and collects the filtrate that is produced by the glomerulus. While Bowman's capsule is involved in the initial filtration of blood in the kidney, it is not directly involved in the regulation of acid-base balance. Once the filtrate is collected in Bowman's capsule, it then passes into the renal tubules where it is modified and processed. Therefore, option B is incorrect because Bowman's capsule is not responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. Option D- Distal tubule: The distal tubule is a part of the renal tubule that comes after the loop of Henle and is responsible for fine-tuning the concentration of urine by reabsorbing some ions and water and secreting others. While the distal tubule plays a role in regulating the balance of electrolytes in the body, it is not primarily responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. The distal tubule does have some capacity to regulate acid-base balance, but its primary function is the regulation of salt and water balance in the body. Therefore, option D is incorrect because the distal tubule is not primarily responsible for regulating acid-base balance in the kidney. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 60-year-old diabetic patient presented to the emergency department with a blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, mildly decreased urine output, and lethargy. On baseline investigations, serum sodium levels were 165mEq/L, blood glucose was 190mg/dl and serum ketones were negative. During the management of this patient, which of the following is an important monitoring step?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old diabetic patient presented to the emergency department with a blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg, mildly decreased urine output, and lethargy. On baseline investigations, serum sodium levels were 165mEq/L, blood glucose was 190mg/dl and serum ketones were negative. During the management of this patient, which of the following is an important monitoring step?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Monitoring signs of cerebral edema: In a patient with hypernatremia, sodium concentration is more than 145mEq/L and serum osmolality is greater which causes fluid to shift from the intracellular compartment and cause the cells to shrink Cells adapt to this change in chronic hypernatremia as in the case of elderly patients in which long-standing decreased oral fluid intake cause this hypernatremia When the patient with hypernatremia is treated then these chronic patients should be managed carefully as the rapid correction of hypernatremia in these patient decreases serum osmolality and cause fluid to shift intracellularly and cells swell up This is most important in the brain as it causes cerebral edema and signs and symptoms of neurologic dysfunction Serum sodium should not be decreased by more than 12mEq/L in 24 hours period and 0.5mEq/L per hour So close monitoring of the patient for every 2 to 4 hours for serum sodium and checking for the signs and symptoms of cerebral edema like seizures or any neurologic dysfunction is important Incorrect Options: Option A- Monitoring blood glucose level: Monitoring blood glucose levels is important in diabetic patients if they present with high blood glucose levels and positive serum ketones to manage the diabetic ketoacidosis If the blood glucose level is mildly elevated and ketones are negative then blood glucose level monitoring is less important than the management of hypernatremia and its complications in these patients Option B- Monitoring serum ketones level: Serum ketones are monitored in patients when the presentation is of diabetic ketoacidosis like the fruity smell of the breath, acidic pH, positive serum ketones, and high blood glucose level level If the blood glucose level is normal and ketones are negative then serum ketones monitoring is unnecessary Option D- Monitoring for urine output: Urine output monitoring is important in severe hypovolemia, decreased blood pressure, and oliguria If the blood pressure and urine output are slightly decreased then monitoring is of secondary importance as compared to monitoring for signs of cerebral edema @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option C- Monitoring signs of cerebral edema:

  • In a patient with hypernatremia, sodium concentration is more than 145mEq/L and serum osmolality is greater which causes fluid to shift from the intracellular compartment and cause the cells to shrink
  • Cells adapt to this change in chronic hypernatremia as in the case of elderly patients in which long-standing decreased oral fluid intake cause this hypernatremia
  • When the patient with hypernatremia is treated then these chronic patients should be managed carefully as the rapid correction of hypernatremia in these patient decreases serum osmolality and cause fluid to shift intracellularly and cells swell up
  • This is most important in the brain as it causes cerebral edema and signs and symptoms of neurologic dysfunction
  • Serum sodium should not be decreased by more than 12mEq/L in 24 hours period and 0.5mEq/L per hour
  • So close monitoring of the patient for every 2 to 4 hours for serum sodium and checking for the signs and symptoms of cerebral edema like seizures or any neurologic dysfunction is important

Incorrect Options:

Option A- Monitoring blood glucose level:

  • Monitoring blood glucose levels is important in diabetic patients if they present with high blood glucose levels and positive serum ketones to manage the diabetic ketoacidosis
  • If the blood glucose level is mildly elevated and ketones are negative then blood glucose level monitoring is less important than the management of hypernatremia and its complications in these patients

Option B- Monitoring serum ketones level:

  • Serum ketones are monitored in patients when the presentation is of diabetic ketoacidosis like the fruity smell of the breath, acidic pH, positive serum ketones, and high blood glucose level level
  • If the blood glucose level is normal and ketones are negative then serum ketones monitoring is unnecessary

Option D- Monitoring for urine output:

  • Urine output monitoring is important in severe hypovolemia, decreased blood pressure, and oliguria
  • If the blood pressure and urine output are slightly decreased then monitoring is of secondary importance as compared to monitoring for signs of cerebral edema

questions.stem: A 54-year-old male presents to the medical emergency department complaining of watery diarrhoea and profuse sweating for the last 12 hours. He reports having had bowel disease over the previous four years. Further evaluation confirms a history of Crohn's disease. He says he has had 8 to 10 episodes of watery diarrhoea since last night. His ECG shows flat T waves and the appearance of U waves. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals alkalosis. What is the most likely metabolic disorder here?
questions.stemHtml: A 54-year-old male presents to the medical emergency department complaining of watery diarrhoea and profuse sweating for the last 12 hours. He reports having had bowel disease over the previous four years. Further evaluation confirms a history of Crohn's disease. He says he has had 8 to 10 episodes of watery diarrhoea since last night. His ECG shows flat T waves and the appearance of U waves. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals alkalosis. What is the most likely metabolic disorder here?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Hypokalemia: The clinical features of watery diarrhoea secondary to Crohn's disease and the appearance of U waves and flat T waves suggest hypokalemia to be the likely metabolic disorder. Hypokalemia (less than three mEq/L or three mmol/L) is a decrease in the serum potassium level. The normal potassium level is 3.5 to 5 mEq/L. Causes of hypokalemia with alkalosis: Vomiting Thiazide and loop diuretics Cushing's syndrome Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) Causes of hypokalemia with acidosis: Diarrhoea Renal tubular acidosis Acetazolamide Partially treated diabetic ketoacidosis Magnesium deficiency may also cause hypokalemia. The investigation includes serum potassium and magnesium levels. ECG changes include: U waves Flat T waves (occasionally inversion) Prolong PR interval ST depression Management includes oral or intravenous potassium administration. Incorrect Options: Option A- Hypercalcemia: Hypercalcemia is a raised calcium level and can present with kidney stones, bone pains, and muscle weakness. A short QT interval resulting from a short ST segment is the most frequent ECG finding in hypercalcemia. Option B- Hyponatremia: Hyponatremia is a sodium level of less than 135 mmol/L. There is low plasma and urine osmolality but no ECG changes. So it is less likely in the case mentioned above. Option D- Hyperkalemia: Hyperkalemia is defined as raised potassium level of more than 5.5mEq/L. In hyperkalemia, ECG shows tall peaked T waves, flattened P waves, prolonged PR interval, ST depression, and prolonged QRS duration. But in the scenario above, ECG has flat T waves suggesting hypokalemia. @Neet_pg_bot

Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for the development of metabolic acidosis in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old female with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with metabolic acidosis. She is being treated with the following medications. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for the development of metabolic acidosis in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Metformin Metformin is a biguanide oral hypoglycemic agent used in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus. The most common side effect of metformin is gastrointestinal disturbance. However, it can also cause lactic acidosis in rare cases, especially in patients with impaired renal function. Metformin-induced lactic acidosis is a type of metabolic acidosis that occurs due to the accumulation of lactic acid in the body. Incorrect options: Option B: Salbutamol Salbutamol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist used in the treatment of asthma and COPD. Trembling, headache, palpitations and muscle cramps are adverse effects of salbutamol. It does not typically cause metabolic acidosis as a side effect. Option C: Ibuprofen Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug ( NSAID ) used for pain relief and inflammation. Interstitial nephritis, gastric ulcer (prostaglandins protect gastric mucosa), renal ischemia (prostaglandins vasodilate afferent arteriole), aplastic anaemia are adverse effects of ibuprofen. It does not typically cause metabolic acidosis as a side effect. Option D: Alendronate Alendronate is a bisphosphonate used for the treatment of osteoporosis and other bone diseases. It does not typically cause metabolic acidosis as a side effect. Esophagitis, osteonecrosis of jaw, and atypical femoral stress fractures are adverse effects of bisphosphonates. @Neet_pg_bot

He has a history of long-term uncontrolled hypertension. The laboratory results showed increased anion gap metabolic acidosis. After an appropriate workup, a diagnosis of renal failure is made. questions.solution: Correct Option B: Accumulation of organic acids Kidneys are the vital organs of the human body that play an important role in the filtration of blood and excretion of metabolic wastes. Kidneys also produce important hormones like vitamin D, erythropoietin, etc. This patient is suffering from metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap. This metabolic acidosis results from the accumulation of organic acids in the body. Some of the causes of renal failure are diabetes, high blood pressure, chronic NSAID users, etc. The accumulation of organic acids is the main reason for the increased anion gap. Some of the symptoms of kidney failure are decreased urine output, fatigue, muscle cramps, fluid overload, nausea, vomiting, dry skin, etc. Incorrect options: Option A: Ketones accumulation Ketone accumulation can also result in an increased anion gap metabolic acidosis but in renal failure, the main cause of metabolic acidosis is the accumulation of organic acids. Ketones are accumulated in the body in diabetes. It is a common condition in type I diabetes mellitus in which insulin is deficient. Option C: Accumulation of salicylates Aspirin is usually used for its analgesic and antiplatelet effect for the management of different diseases. The aspirin is also called salicylates. The salicylate overdose can result in metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap but in renal failure, the main cause of metabolic acidosis is the accumulation of organic acids. It can also cause respiratory alkalosis initially because of the increased respiratory drive. Option D: Accumulation of formate Methanol is an alcohol that is used in antifreeze, perfumes, carburetor cleaners, etc. Methanol toxicity occurs because of unintentional ingestion of methanol. The methanol is converted into formaldehyde by alcohol dehydrogenase. The formaldehyde is further converted into formate by the aldehyde dehydrogenase. It can also cause increased anion gap metabolic acidosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male patient presented in the outpatient department with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness. The laboratory results revealed low pH, decreased bicarbonate ions, and high potassium. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type 4 is made. Which of the following is the cause of the above-mentioned patient's condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old male patient presented in the outpatient department with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness. The laboratory results revealed low pH, decreased bicarbonate ions, and high potassium. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type 4 is made. Which of the following is the cause of the above-mentioned patient's condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Hypoaldosteronism: Hypoaldosteronism is a condition in which there is a deficiency of aldosterone. Normally the activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system leads to the activation of aldosterone. The collecting duct of the nephron is the main site where the aldosterone acts. Normally aldosterone causes the excretion of hydrogen and potassium ions. However, in renal tubular acidosis type 4, there is a deficiency of aldosterone or aldosterone resistance, which results in hyperkalemia. Hyperkalemia can be fatal to the heart and can result in life-threatening arrhythmias. With hyperkalemia, ECG changes can occur. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hyperaldosteronism: Hyperaldosteronism is the excessive aldosterone production that results in excessive excretion of potassium and hydrogen ions. As a result, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis is seen in such patients. Option C - ADH deficiency: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) acts on vasopressin receptors that cause the expression of receptors in the distal part of nephrons causing the reabsorption of water. In ADH deficiency, there is insufficient ADH which results in excessive excretion of water leading to decreased urine osmolality and high serum osmolarity. Option D - SIADH: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone is a condition in which there is excessive retention of water due to excess ADH. The urine osmolality is high and there is hypervolemia. Some of the causes of SIADH are meningitis, encephalitis, brain tumors, psychosis, lung disease, etc. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A: Lisinopril Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor medication that is commonly used in the treatment of CKD. It acts by blocking the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. By inhibiting angiotensin II, lisinopril reduces aldosterone secretion and promotes sodium and water excretion, which can lead to hyperkalemia. Angiotensin II specifically constrict the efferent arteriole and increases the glomerular filtration pressure, and increases the proteinuria. One of the therapeutic effects of ACE inhibitors is reducing proteinuria by dilating the efferent arteriole and thus decreasing the filtration pressure, which ultimately leads to reduced proteinuria, which is a common complication of CKD. Incorrect options: Option B: Hydrochlorothiazide Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic medication that can help reduce blood pressure in patients with hypertension and CKD. It decreases sodium reabsorption and therefore decreases fluid reabsorption; this directly causes decreased levels of circulating sodium. It does not have a significant effect on reducing proteinuria. Option C: Amlodipine Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker medication that can help reduce blood pressure in patients with hypertension and CKD. It does not have a significant effect on reducing proteinuria. Option D: Spironolactone Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic medication that can also reduce blood pressure in patients with CKD. It has no effect on reducing proteinuria. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A child was brought with complaints of high fever, multiple seizures, headache, and neck rigidity. CSF analysis showed low glucose, high protein, and many polymorphs. The CSF culture showed pleomorphic gram-negative bacilli. What is true about the causative organism?
questions.stemHtml: A child was brought with complaints of high fever, multiple seizures, headache, and neck rigidity. CSF analysis showed low glucose, high protein, and many polymorphs. The CSF culture showed pleomorphic gram-negative bacilli. What is true about the causative organism?

options.label: B
options.text: Produces non-lactose fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar

options.label: C
options.text: Exhibits satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus colonies

options.label: D
options.text: It exhibits alpha hemolysis on sheep blood agar

questions.answerText: Exhibits satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus colonies
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Exhibits satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus colonies: The child is suffering from meningitis. Common causes of meningitis in a child is due to Haemophilus influenza, Neisseria meningitidis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Among these organisms, the only pleomorphic, gram-negative bacilli is Haemophilus influenzae. Satellitism refers to a phenomenon where one bacterium grows around or near another bacterium, usually relying on the nutrients produced by the other bacterium. Haemophilus influenzae exhibits satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus colonies. Haemophilus influenzae requires factors like factor V and factor X produced by Staphylococcus aureus due to hemolysis of the RBCs. Therefore, it grows around the colonies of Staphylococcus aureus on culture media. Incorrect Options: Option A - It is bacitracin sensitive: Bacitracin sensitivity is typically used to differentiate different strains of Streptococcus, particularly in the context of respiratory infections such as pharyngitis. Option B - Produces non-lactose fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar: This characteristic is more indicative of Enterobacteriaceae, which are gram-negative bacteria that typically ferment lactose and produce pink/red colonies on MacConkey agar. Option D - It exhibits alpha hemolysis on sheep blood agar: Alpha hemolysis refers to a partial breakdown of red blood cells, resulting in a greenish discoloration of the agar around the colonies. This characteristic is commonly seen in Streptococcus pneumoniae, a gram-positive bacterium and one of the leading causes of bacterial meningitis. @Neet_pg_bot
